Projet de loi de finances rectificative au Sénégal : un duel à quitte ou double. Face à des députés Pastef hostiles, le Premier ministre Ahmadou Al Aminou Lô aura fort à faire, ce 27 octobre, pour que soit adopté par l’Assemblée nationale un projet de loi de finances rectificative crucial.

Sahara occidental : 5 questions pour comprendre les intentions des États-Unis avant le vote du 31 octobre. À quelques jours des élections américaines de mi-mandat, Washington veut faire adopter une résolution qui accélérerait le règlement du conflit et transformerait radicalement la Minurso. Mais à ce stade les obstacles à un accord restent nombreux.

Soutenu par l’Union africaine, le Togolais Gilbert Houngbo réussira-t-il à conserver la tête de l’OIT ?. Candidat à sa propre succession à la tête de l’Organisation internationale du travail (OIT), le Togolais Gilbert Houngbo affrontera deux rivaux venus d’Espagne et du Pérou. Soutenu par l’Union africaine, il défend son bilan malgré une sévère crise budgétaire.

Tchad-Niger : une nouvelle escalade entre Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno et Abdourahamane Tiani. Niamey accuse N’Djamena d’avoir lancé une frappe de drone sur son territoire, avec le soutien de la France. Une charge qui ravive la méfiance entre les deux voisins.

Restructuration du conseil d’administration et soupçons de conflits d’intérêts : que se passe-t-il chez Ecobank ?. L’annulation de l’assemblée générale d’Ecobank du 26 octobre à la dernière minute ravive les inquiétudes des petits actionnaires. Entre soupçons de conflits d’intérêts du président du conseil d’administration et reprise en main par Alain Nkontchou, décryptage d’une gouvernance sous pression.

Fédération algérienne de football : trois anciens présidents lourdement condamnés. Le procès concernant la gestion financière de la Fédération algérienne de football de 2017 à 2023 a abouti à des peines sévères pour les trois anciens présidents de l’instance durant cette période. Le verdict a été prononcé ce 27 octobre.

Dessalement et hydrogène : la grande transformation verte du marocain OCP. Le géant marocain des engrais phosphatés a lancé un vaste plan d’investissements verts en 2022. Si les progrès sont tangibles, la question du financement reste un enjeu majeur.

RDC – Delly Sesanga : « Le report des élections ne peut pas devenir le programme implicite du pouvoir ». Le président d’Envol revient pour Jeune Afrique sur la création d’une nouvelle rébellion dirigée par Joseph Kabila. Il évoque aussi les critiques visant la faible mobilisation des adversaires du chef de l’État Félix Tshisekedi et refuse toute transition qui maintiendrait ce dernier au pouvoir.

De la Kabylie à Paris, la longue marche du MAK d’Aksel Bellabbaci et Ferhat Mehenni. Aksel Bellabbaci a découvert la colère kabyle adolescent, avant de devenir l’un des cadres du Mouvement pour l’autodétermination de la Kabylie (MAK). Son parcours raconte la stratégie de son chef, Ferhat Mehenni, ses espoirs et la répression qui les a frappés.

Mali : que sont devenus les anciens ténors de la classe politique ?. Depuis le coup d’État de 2020, les anciennes figures des partis désormais dissous ont connu des fortunes diverses. Entre ralliement, disgrâce et démêlés judiciaires, ils peinent à trouver leur place dans le Mali d’Assimi Goïta.

Il y a dix ans, la mort de Mouhcine Fikri mettait le feu au Rif. Malheureux accident à l’origine, la mort du poissonnier d’Al Hoceïma a donné lieu à l’un des principaux mouvements de révolte qu’a connu le Maroc ces dernières années : le Hirak du Rif.

Élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis : qui sont les candidats issus de la diaspora africaine ?. Sept candidats d’origine africaine se lancent à la conquête de la Chambre des représentants, alors que les communautés immigrées font face à une hostilité de plus en plus virulente encouragée par des mesures de répression musclées.

Bola Tinubu a-t-il réussi à mettre l’économie nigériane en ordre de marche ?. Dans un pays longtemps hanté par le spectre de l’effondrement, les liens économiques entre banques, industriels et investisseurs se renforcent. Pour le chef de l’État, l’épreuve consiste à transformer ce mouvement en prospérité partagée.

Sommet Russie-Afrique : ce que révèle le plan d’action confidentiel de Moscou. Alors que le sommet Russie-Afrique s’ouvre ce 28 octobre, le projet de plan d’action 2027-2029 de Moscou a fuité. De l’alignement des votes à l’ONU au secteur minier, analyse d’une feuille de route qui cherche à renforcer l’influence russe sur le continent.

« Une réalisation historique pour l’Afrique » : Aliko Dangote boucle l’introduction en Bourse de sa raffinerie. L’homme d’affaires nigérian a clôturé l’opération deux semaines après la date initialement prévue. Il estime avoir levé « plus de trois ou quatre fois » les 1,6 milliard de dollars visés.

Amine Bouabid, le banquier à poigne qui porte l’essor africain de Bank of Africa. Le directeur général exécutif de Bank of Africa en charge de l’Afrique dirige les vingt filiales avec franc-parler, goût du risque et obsession des résultats. Une méthode forgée aux États-Unis et éprouvée au Maroc, qu’il assume jusque dans ses rapports avec les politiques.

Le Gabon rétablit les réseaux sociaux après huit mois de suspension. Le gouvernement a également rendu l’identification formelle obligatoire pour tous les usagers gabonais en octobre, mettant ainsi fin à l’anonymat en ligne dans le pays.

En République démocratique du Congo, les Kabila, rebelles de père en fils. Contraint à l’exil et condamné à mort, Joseph Kabila a pris, le 12 octobre, la tête de la rébellion politico-militaire dans l’est de la RDC, dénonçant la « tyrannie » de l’actuel président, Félix Tshisekedi. Un bagage insurrectionnel hérité de son père et prédécesseur, Laurent-Désiré Kabila.

En Tanzanie, l’opposant Tundu Lissu menace d’entamer une grève de la faim pour protester contre ses conditions de détention. L’homme politique de 58 ans, incarcéré depuis un an et demi pour avoir exigé une réforme du système électoral, était retourné dans son pays en 2023 après plusieurs années d’exil. Il risque la peine de mort.

En Algérie, la réhabilitation inachevée de Krim Belkacem, icône de la guerre d’indépendance. La célébration de l’anniversaire de la mort du « Lion des djebels » rencontre un écho croissant dans la presse algérienne. Un tel regain d’intérêt, s’il élude les circonstances de son assassinat en octobre 1970 à Francfort, en Allemagne, par des tueurs venus d’Alger, traduit une volonté d’élargir les assises mémorielles du régime.

En Algérie, le Parlement autorise l’envoi d’unités militaires au Niger. Le déploiement de l’armée algérienne sur le théâtre nigérien, validé dimanche par les députés et les sénateurs, enterre plus de six décennies de doctrine de non-intervention du pays hors de ses frontières. Il promet de reconfigurer les équilibres stratégiques au Sahel.

Comment des « prêts toxiques » chinois ont alimenté une spirale de surendettement en Zambie. Des documents bancaires confidentiels révèlent que des prêts de la Banque industrielle et commerciale de Chine ont contribué à étouffer financièrement le pays africain.

Le Ghanéen Ibrahim Mahama cultive un art sans limites du partage. Numéro un au dernier classement des personnalités les plus influentes du monde de l’art, l’artiste ghanéen de 39 ans reste méconnu du grand public. Rencontre à Tamale, dans le nord du Ghana, en amont de sa première grande exposition en France, à la Fondation Cartier.

Le Ghana sème objets et fantômes du colonialisme à la Fondation Cartier. Pour son exposition « Le Temps des récoltes », l’artiste ghanéen Ibrahim Mahama a invité à jouer neuf acteurs de la création contemporaine. Le fruit de cette énergie collective s’expose sur trois niveaux où l’enchevêtrement de formes et de matériaux tend le miroir au champ politique.

Cinquante ans après l’« indépendance » du Transkei, l’Afrique du Sud n’en a pas fini avec l’héritage des bantoustans. Proclamé « indépendant » par Pretoria le 26 octobre 1976, ce territoire du Cap-Oriental a légué à l’Afrique du Sud démocratique des administrations défaillantes, dont la mauvaise gouvernance pèse encore sur la région à l’approche des élections municipales du 4 novembre.

En Crète, quinze mineurs soudanais accusés d’être des passeurs sont acquittés. Dans la loi grecque, tout migrant accusé d’avoir conduit un canot ou un véhicule transportant d’autres migrants encourt une peine minimale de dix ans de prison. Alors que les arrivées depuis la Libye ne cessent d’augmenter depuis quelques années, de plus en plus de migrants en subissent les conséquences.

Ces lobbys évangéliques américains qui exportent leur guerre culturelle en Afrique. « En Afrique, la vague réactionnaire » (1/4). Profitant du discours en vogue sur le continent autour des « valeurs traditionnelles africaines » menacées par la « perversion » de l’Occident, la droite évangélique américaine a su exporter son idéologie ultraconservatrice auprès de certains dirigeants africains.

Côte d’Ivoire : un an après la réélection d’Alassane Ouattara, une scène politique cadenassée. Les principaux partis de l’opposition ivoirienne, dont plusieurs responsables ont été convoqués par la justice, se disent victimes d’un « harcèlement » de la part du pouvoir.

Soudan : plus de vingt morts après une attaque de drone contre un marché à Nyala. L’armée soudanaise mène régulièrement des attaques sur cette ville, où les Forces de soutien rapide ont instauré une autorité rivale de celle du gouvernement reconnu par la communauté internationale.

Au Nigeria, les orpailleurs morts en détention ont subi « des traitements cruels, inhumains et dégradants », selon une commission d’enquête. Des survivants avaient raconté à l’Agence France-Presse avoir été entassés dans des cellules mal ventilées, l’un d’eux faisant aussi état de l’usage d’un gaz par les gardiens.

Ebola : plus de 10 000 cas recensés en Afrique, la grande majorité en RDC, et 4 887 morts. Quelque 2 684 guérisons ont été recensées, mais le taux de létalité est proche des 50 %. L’épidémie s’est propagée dans plusieurs autres régions du continent, avec des cas signalés au Kenya et jusqu’en Afrique de l’Ouest au Nigeria.

Ethiopie : 36 000 personnes ont fui au Kenya, en raison des affrontements dans le sud du pays. Le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies pour les réfugiés souligne que l’aide alimentaire est la priorité, avec un besoin urgent d’eau potable, d’abris, d’installations sanitaires et de soins de santé.

Les banques de développement de nouveau à l’assaut du secteur minier. La Banque mondiale a annoncé, mi-octobre, qu’elle soutiendrait des projets d’industrie extractive dans huit pays, dont quatre en Afrique. Le secteur intéresse de plus en plus les institutions d’aide au développement.

Egypte : la journaliste Lina Attalah, directrice du média indépendant « Mada Masr », libérée après le paiement d’une amende. A l’issue d’une unique audience, un tribunal a ordonné la fermeture du site Internet et imposé une amende de près de 49 000 euros, pour l’avoir exploité « sans licence ». Il s’agit de la sixième affaire visant Lina Attalah et le média « Mada Masr » en six ans, mais aucune n’avait jusque-là abouti à un procès.

Tunisie : un journaliste indépendant, critique virulent du président, condamné à quatre ans de prison. De nombreux opposants et journalistes tunisiens font face à une vague de répression accrue depuis 2021.

En Afrique, l’homophobie érigée en politique d’Etat. « En Afrique, la vague réactionnaire » (2/4). Souvent présentées comme une réponse à une « attaque culturelle » venue de l’Occident, les législations homophobes se multiplient sur le continent, avec pour conséquence des discriminations et des violences en hausse, tandis que la lutte contre l’épidémie de sida est affaiblie.

The foreign ministers of Egypt and Saudi Arabia spoke via phone about efforts to manage and prevent escalation in the ongoing regional crisis. They emphasized the importance of ongoing consultation and coordination.

An unidentified minor was shot dead after attacking a police officer with knives outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade. The assailant shouted ‘Allahu Akbar’ during the incident, raising Serbia’s terrorism threat level.

​​​​Morocco: Ten years after the Rif uprising, its leaders are still jailed and its demands unmet Submitted by Renee Boskaljon on Wed, 10/28/2026 - 08:01 A decade after fishmonger Mouhcine Fikri’s death triggered widespread protests, economic hardship and repression persist across the marginalised region Moroccans take part in a candlelight vigil in Casablanca on 8 August 2017 for a protestor who died in the Rif protests in northern Morocco after he was hit in the head during clashes with security forces (Stringer/AFP) Off “Our family has been through a lot. My mother’s health has deteriorated, but despite everything, she continues to hold on.” Mohamed Ahamjik has done everything he can to help his family since his younger brother, Nabil, was arrested in 2017 over his role in Morocco ’s Rif protest movement. He is serving a 20-year prison sentence. Since then, Mohamed has worked to raise awareness about his case. “This has always been a duty towards my mother, my brother Nabil and our family,” he told Middle East Eye, speaking ahead of Wednesday’s anniversary marking a decade since protests erupted in the kingdom’s northern Rif mountains over poverty, marginalisation and underdevelopment. The movement was sparked by the death of fishmonger Mouhcine Fikri, who was crushed inside a rubbish truck in Al Hoceima on 28 October 2016 while trying to retrieve his confiscated catch. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ten years on, the wounds left by repression and decades of marginalisation are still felt across the region, while six prominent Hirak figures remain in prison, including the movement's leader Nasser Zefzafi, who was sentenced to 20 years. According to Moroccan historian Maati Monjib, the Rif uprising was “one of the most significant social movements” in Morocco since King Mohammed VI ascended the throne in 1999. Initially centered in Al Hoceima and its surrounding province, the protests were tolerated for several months before authorities launched a crackdown in late May, resulting in hundreds of arrests. Authorities branded the movement as separatist - a label Monjib described as “false accusations made to discredit their demands”. He told MEE that although a small minority of activists expressed separatist views, mostly in Facebook groups, the main leaders who remain imprisoned never did. The state’s response reached a new turning point on 20 July, when riot police used tear gas and batons to disperse demonstrators in Al Hoceima, severely injuring 22‑year‑old Imad el‑Attabi, who died the following month. The crackdown triggered widespread solidarity protests across Morocco throughout the summer of 2017. An uprising against ‘hogra’ Nabil played an important role in the movement. His activism, Mohamed told MEE, was driven by his rejection of “hogra”, a term referring to humiliation and oppression, and by what he saw as “the historical injustice that the region suffered for decades from the central power”. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); His arrest did not come as a surprise to his family. “After the parliamentary majority falsely accused the Rif movement of separatism, we understood that a vast wave of arrests was being prepared,” Mohamed said. ‘After the parliamentary majority falsely accused the Rif movement of separatism, we understood that a vast wave of arrests was being prepared’ - Mohamed Ahamjik, brother of a jailed Rif activist Transferred between several prisons over the years, Nabil is now held in Tangier. From his cell, he wrote a master’s thesis on the Rif’s relationship with the state at Mohammed I University in Oujda, earning an 18 out of 20 and a recommendation for publication. Now a doctoral student, he staged a 10‑day hunger strike last month after authorities denied him a proper space to work on his PhD. In recent years, rights groups have denounced the arrests of Rif protesters, along with allegations of torture , ill-treatment in custody and violations of fair-trial standards. The crackdown did not stop with those who took to the streets. Journalists who covered the protests and activists living abroad were also caught up in the wave of repression. Said El Amrani, a digital creator, former journalist and human rights activist, is one of them. Born in the Rif, he moved to Belgium in the 1990s to pursue his studies. In 1991, he was briefly arrested upon his arrival at Tangier airport for his activism. In 2016, two months before the outbreak of the Rif protests, he returned to the region for what would be the last time. As the crackdown extended to the diaspora, he and other activists have not returned since. “Since the beginning of the Rif movement, at least 11 activists have been arrested when arriving in Morocco. Two of them were sentenced to prison, one of them is still in jail,” El Amrani told MEE, adding that like many other activists in the diaspora, he has also been targeted online. “Photos were taken from my personal social media account, including pictures of my younger daughter, manipulated to create sexualised images, and then shared on Facebook.” He has also been repeatedly targeted by a news outlet reportedly close to Morocco’s intelligence services. Today, he told MEE, the region remains under tight security. “They built at least five new police stations since the protests,” he said. A history of revolt and repression Over the past century, the history of the Rif has been marked by resistance and repression. Jamal El Khattabi, born in Al Hoceima in the early 1960s, grew up on stories of armed struggle and of relatives killed in the Rif War, the anti‑colonial uprising fought from 1921 to 1926 between Berber tribes of the Rif and Spanish - later French - colonial forces. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); His father was among the young fighters who joined Abdelkrim El Khattabi, the leader of the resistance movement who united the Rif’s tribes and proclaimed an independent republic in 1921. It took the combined forces of France and Spain to crush the uprising in 1926, marking the end of the self-proclaimed republic. On his mother’s side, El Khattabi’s grandfather died before she was born. The family was told he had suffocated after exposure to chemical weapons used by the Spanish to squash the resistance. An undated picture taken in Cairo in February 1948 of Abdelkrim El Khattabi, left, former leader of the Rif rebellion, with his brother Mohamed Khattab (J. Weinberg/AFP) The repression did not end with his parents’ generation. After Morocco gained independence from French and Spanish colonial rule in 1956, the army under Crown Prince Hassan, later King Hassan II, brutally suppressed uprisings in several regions, including the Rif. Jamal, who joined activist groups during university, was arrested twice under Hassan II, who was known for ruling with an iron fist. After his first arrest in 1989, he was beaten with a thick stick and thrown from a roof, leaving him with a serious back injury. He described being taken blindfolded to Derb Moulay Cherif in Casablanca, where the torture included severe beatings, threats involving dogs and prolonged exposure to bright lights. “I could no longer stand without them having to ‘help’ me,” he told MEE. After his second detention, he fled Morocco for Spain and eventually settled in the Netherlands. When Mohammed VI took the throne in 1999 after his father’s death, the kingdom appeared to be entering a more open era, with promises of reform, and the years of political persecution, torture and enforced disappearances seemed to be over. The Arab Spring protests of 2011 led to constitutional changes that formally limited the monarchy’s powers, but hopes for lasting political reform soon began to fade. Repression intensified in the years that followed, becoming particularly pronounced after the Rif protests. Over the past decade, numerous reports have shown how the monarchy crushes dissent, increasingly relying on surveillance technologies - including the Israeli spyware Pegasus - as well as defamation campaigns and unfair trials. The worsening crackdown was stark during last year’s Gen Z protests over failing public services, unemployment and corruption, even as billions were poured into stadiums for the 2030 World Cup. While the Rif protests were initially tolerated for months, the Gen Z demonstrations were crushed within weeks: 6,000 people were arrested, most of them in the first days. A year later, around 700 remain in jail, including dozens of minors, according to the Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH). ‘They have no future’ The memory of the Rif uprising a decade ago has taken on new relevance amid a turbulent year for Morocco. While the kingdom has experienced rapid economic growth and made history last month with the election of its first female prime minister, deep economic and social frustrations remain. Youth unemployment, at 37 percent, and rising living costs are among the deepest issues. Those frustrations came into sharp focus again this summer, when tens of thousands of people attempted to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Many of them were young Moroccans from the Rif region. ‘There continues to be a deep desire for dignity and equal recognition - where a Moroccan, in the Rif or elsewhere, should be the equal of every other Moroccan, regardless of status or background’ - Maati Monjib, historian While Atlantic cities such as Casablanca, Rabat and Tangier, and tourist hotspots like Marrakech, have drawn billions in investment and gleaming new infrastructure, the Rif and other impoverished regions like the Atlas Mountains have been left on the margins. The Rif has the highest number of cancer patients in Morocco, a toll linked to the chemical bombs Spain dropped during the Rif War. Yet the hospitals and specialised equipment that could treat patients lie hours away. This mirrors a wider divide, one that shaped the debate in the recent elections: a Morocco of two speeds. In Tangier, the Tanger Med port, industrial zones, car factories and booming exports drive rapid growth. In the Rif, young people still face high unemployment and few prospects. The state did respond to some of the protesters’ demands: a new faculty affiliated with the University of Tetouan was opened. But in El Amrani’s view, most initiatives fall short. A hospital was recently built, “but there is not enough medical staff”. For young people, “there is no work,” he added. “Many have left, most of them clandestinely for Europe. Others have moved to Moroccan cities such as Tangier and Tetouan.” For decades, thousands of families in the borderlands lived off the informal trade that flowed through the Spanish autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla. In recent years, as controls on the borders with the Spanish enclaves tightened, that trade became impossible. That left the borderlands poorer and pushed more and more young people to risk their lives to reach Europe, as the latest mass attempt to cross to Ceuta this summer showed. “They have nothing to lose,” El Amrani said. Many are out of school, without work and without access to healthcare. “They feel they have no future. For them, the only solution is to leave.” Monjib, who himself spent three months in prison for his activism and is now routinely targeted by the authorities, told MEE that although heavy state repression largely paralysed the Rif movement and shifted its focus toward demanding the release of political prisoners, its core pursuit of equality endures. “There continues to be a deep desire for dignity and equal recognition - where a Moroccan, in the Rif or elsewhere, should be the equal of every other Moroccan, regardless of status or background,” he said. How UK antisemitism report could worsen the very problem it warns against Submitted by Gary Spedding on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 15:37 The government risks teaching Jewish pupils that support for Israel is integral to their identity, and that Palestine solidarity is inherently threatening UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell speaks in Liverpool on 27 September 2026 (Darren Staples/AFP) Off Last week, Education Secretary Lucy Powell accepted Sir David Bell’s review into antisemitism in British schools and colleges. While billed as “independent”, this does not appear to be a neutral examination of prejudice against Jewish pupils. Rather, it is a document shaped by what appears to be undeclared ties between UK and Israeli educational and advocacy networks; an undue emphasis on Palestine solidarity as intimidatory and problematic; and a near-exclusive reliance on the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)’s working definition of antisemitism . The definition’s appended examples disproportionately target and chill speech about Israel. The review found that almost three in five Jewish students between the ages of 16 and 19 reported that they had experienced or witnessed antisemitism , rising from about one in five overall. This is an alarming statistic. Yet the study itself notes that the claim rests on a “low sample size of 92 students who identify as Jewish” within a survey of more than 5,000 people. The data simply does not justify the findings. By treating antisemitism as a form of racism requiring politicised safeguarding and wider adoption of the IHRA definition, the review risks weaponising antisemitism against Palestine solidarity in education . Further, by addressing antisemitism in isolation from broader conversations about racism, and by restricting support for Palestine, Britain risks alienating students and worsening antisemitism in our schools. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Bell’s appointment as an “independent” reviewer sits uneasily with his background. He previously served as permanent secretary at the Department for Education and chief inspector of schools in England. He is listed as having sat on the National Council of the Academic Study Group on Israel and the Middle East, whose mission is to “initiate or expand active links and research collaboration between academics, specialists and centres-of-excellence in the UK and their counterparts in Israel”. Its director, John Levy , has longstanding ties to the Friends of Israel Educational Foundation and Academic Friends of Israel . These connections should have prompted the Department for Education to question Bell’s impartiality - yet none of this appears to have been formally declared as a conflict of interest. It is also notable that, in 2005, Bell was accused of Islamophobia while head of Ofsted, after he said that Muslim schools risked undermining social cohesion. Criticism reframed Based on my own extensive research, I believe the composition of the review’s reference group raises further concerns about impartiality and neutrality, as the organisational links of some members highlight a substantial, institutionalised ecosystem shaping what many Jewish pupils encounter on Israel and Jewish identity. These are not abstract associations, yet they receive next to no scrutiny. Israel advocacy organisations, and educational charities with explicit pro-Israel missions, deliver talks, workshops, resources, and engagement programmes to thousands of students nationwide. Such programmes explicitly seek to cultivate emotional attachment, associate Jewish identity with support for Israel, and encourage Jewish pupils to actively advocate for the country. Attempts to reframe as antisemitic any criticism of Israel or solidarity with Palestinians, places Jewish pupils at the forefront of a fraught battle they largely did not choose. Such discourse frames Jewish identity as requiring support for Israel, while Palestine solidarity is cast as a hostile, existential threat. If the government restricts Palestine solidarity in schools by using antisemitism as a convenient scapegoat, the backlash could have dire consequences The exploitation of legitimate fears and vulnerabilities, whereby young Jews are encouraged to feel intimidated by expressions of support for Palestinian rights, has been examined in documentaries such as Israelism . The access that Israel advocacy organisations have to schools should raise serious concerns about neutrality in the opposite direction, particularly given their potential to promote negative tropes and stereotypes about Palestine and Palestinians. In a similar vein, one of the review’s most alarming outputs is its reinforcement of the notion that Palestine solidarity is inherently linked to antisemitism. This polarisation of discussion around the UK’s genuine antisemitism problem is dangerous. Many leftists, who should be natural allies of oppressed minorities, are so fed up with having Palestine solidarity denounced as antisemitic that they shut down when it comes to tackling actual antisemitism. If the government restricts Palestine solidarity in schools by using antisemitism as a convenient scapegoat, the backlash could have dire consequences, not least for Jewish students facing genuine antisemitism. This could hamper efforts to implement a coherent strategy. Indeed, efforts to combat antisemitism are far more successful when bigotry is tackled through intersectional approaches that allow every student to feel seen, while simultaneously learning about the specific, devastating and lethal history of anti-Jewish oppression. Educators can highlight Jewish historical trauma not to minimise others’ experiences, but to build deep, empathetic connections across cultural and ethnic boundaries. Middle East Eye reached out to Bell and the Department for Education for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Political pressure I would go so far as to warn that political pressure seeking to exploit antisemitism to shield Israel from criticism threatens to strip away the infrastructure needed to combat it. This further undermines meaningful efforts to tackle hatred of Jews. When allegations of antisemitism are weaponised to excuse Israel’s crimes, a question mark is placed over those reporting it, in a way that victims of other forms of racism do not face. When a Jewish person reports experiencing antisemitism today, observers might wonder: was this actual antisemitism, or have they been taught to view Palestine solidarity and anti-Zionism as anti-Jewish hatred and a personal attack? This chilling effect, already felt in free speech and the exploration of Palestine-related issues, also threatens the fight against antisemitism. It risks encouraging dismissive attitudes towards anti-Jewish prejudice, hatred and oppression. Let’s be crystal clear: antisemitism is real, pervasive, cyclical and pernicious. Jews should not have to fight this blight alone, and Jewish children must be protected as an absolute priority. We can acknowledge that antisemitism is a growing problem in our schools and society, while guarding against its weaponisation in the context of Palestine solidarity. Antisemitism reviewer David Bell said Muslim schools could threaten UK's 'coherence' Read More » In 2024, the Institute for Jewish Policy Research found that 23 percent of parents reported their child had experienced antisemitism directly at school, in the vicinity of school, or travelling to or from school. This is not insignificant, but it is far below the figures published in the Bell review. The review’s framing worryingly subordinates classic antisemitic abuse - Hitler salutes, Holocaust jokes, money stereotypes, physical assaults, isolation and intimidation - to concerns about Palestine solidarity badges, flags, symbols and “political expression”. An analysis by Newscord , examining the review’s text, found that roughly a quarter of it concerns Israel, Palestine or political expression. The terms of reference effectively locked in the IHRA approach from the outset, precluding consideration of alternative definitions that do not focus so heavily on criticism of Israel. Many responses to the call for evidence, including 158 critical of the review itself or of the use of the IHRA definition, were not meaningfully reflected or quoted. In addition, despite the review identifying “confusion around the boundary between legitimate political expression and antisemitism”, a majority of those directly asked - 526 out of 590 - said they could distinguish between the two. This finding was omitted from the main report. The government risks teaching Jewish pupils that support for Israel is integral to their identity, and that Palestine solidarity, or criticism of Israeli policy, is inherently threatening to them as Jews. It also risks teaching non-Jewish students that their Jewish classmates see Israel as integral to their identity, and that suggesting otherwise is deeply racist. This reinforces, rather than challenges, the harmful assumption that Jewish students must “ support or have views on the state of Israel ” because of their Jewish identity - ironically, something the report itself confirms causes deep discomfort among Jewish pupils and staff. FOOTBALL: THE NOT SO FUNNY MONEY SAGAS. Who said international breaks are boring? Actually, I said that. In my defence, however, they generally are quite boring, even with the new Nations League tournament. The first international break of the 2026/27 season, a daunting three weeks spanning the end of September, proved different though. It produced stories so spicy, there was a meme circulating across social media that ‘we don’t want club football to return.’ MANCHESTER CITY’S COLOSSAL MESS The first and the most significant bombshell dropped when the anonymous third party commission investigating Manchester City and the 115 charges of financial irregularity levied on them by the Premier League delivered its verdict against City. The 115 charges consisted primarily of the club failing to provide accurate financial information pertaining to inflows and outflows, namely revenues and payments to players and managers. Other charges were merely implications of the former, namely, breaching multiple articles of the Premier League’s Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) and UEFA’s Financial Fair Play (FFP) regulations. Finally, there were about 35 charges of the club not cooperating with investigators and withholding information. The commission found Manchester City guilty on 114 of the 115 charges. The financial impropriety charges against Manchester City and FC Barcelona have the potential to rewrite the history books and change the two biggest football leagues on the planet. Here’s why Now how did we get here? A slight recap. In 2008, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan bought Manchester City after its previous owners were caught in a corruption case in Thailand. He’s the son of UAE’s founding father, Sheikh Zayed. And as is customary in that part of the world, Sheikh Mansour serves as the Vice President and Deputy Prime Minister of UAE, while his brother is the current President. Being the Vice President comes with its perks: Mansour oversees the Central Bank of the UAE and the Emirates Investment Authority. You can guess where I’m going with this. Manchester City invested heavily in its squad soon after the takeover, bringing in the likes of David Silva, Yaya Toure and Sergio Aguero. Big players soon brought in trophies, the pinnacle being that ‘Agueroooo’ goal to clinch the Premier League title for 2011/12. This soon became a normal — City has won eight league titles out of 14 since 2012, along with seven EFL Cups, four FA Cups and a UEFA Champions League. In 2018, the German investigative magazine Der Spiegel published a report detailing financial irregularities in the City infrastructure, obtained through phishing attacks carried out by hackers. City refused to comment on “out-of-context materials purportedly stolen.” An investigation by UEFA brought about a two-year ban from European competition, which was overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). Then came the independent commission formed by the Premier League’s Judicial Panel, which took three years to come to their decision. Manchester City was, according to the findings of the commission, deploying sham contracts, which essentially ballooned up sponsorship deals on paper without getting that revenue. The delta? Funnelled in by the Sheikh. Similarly, some officials and players were paid more than what City’s financial books stated. Again, the delta being paid off by the Sheikh. In an age where FFP rules dictate a club cannot spend more than it earns, and where clubs like Everton are docked 10 points by the Premier League for a £20 million overspend, a question pops up: how did City get away with alleged gross misreporting of more than £900 million for over a decade? There are two things to bear in mind here. For the most part of the decade, Gianni Infantino was the General Secretary of UEFA. It is rumoured that he used his influence to sweep everything under the carpet, making sure no anomaly makes it to the media. The hacks that led to Der Spiegel’s report contain email correspondence between Infantino and Khaldoon Al Mubarak, an Emirati statesperson appointed chairman of Manchester City. The most powerful man in world football approved, facilitated and helped protect the blatant smash-and-grab by the sheikhs, most famously covering up FFP breaches by City in 2014. Secondly, the rise of City closely mirrors that of current British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Burnham is Mancunian and served as the mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 till he became prime minister in 2026. During his mayorship, he attended hospitality dinners with Al Mubarak, supervised official contracts with companies owned by Sheikh Mansour, and saw the UAE pump millions in real estate and economic development, in line with his vision to eradicate homelessness. He even showed public support to Manchester City on an official tour to Japan. And now as prime minister, he has issued a statement saying he hopes the Emiratis do not pull investments from Manchester as a result of the guilty verdict. Manchester City has filed an appeal against the decision of the independent commission, claiming clear material errors of law, principle and fact. The result of the appeal is expected in the first quarter of 2027, with huge implications regardless of the outcome. If the decision is upheld, City could possibly be stripped of all their titles since the UAE takeover, fined, and relegated to the lower divisions, which would spell the end of the club as it is. If the decision is reversed, it would probably just confirm to many the modern reality that deep pockets always prevail. BARCELONA’S REFEREEING MESS The second major news from the international break featured FC Barcelona and the infamous Negreira case. The Negreira case centres on payments worth €7.4 million made by Barcelona between 2001 and 2018 to the official bank accounts of companies owned by Jose Enriquez Negreira, then serving as the vice president of the Technical Committee of Referees of the Spanish Football Federation. The payments coincide with a period wherein Barcelona was accused of benefitting from preferential refereeing. Both the club and the individual deny allegations of bribing and sports corruption, maintaining that the payments were for analytics and refereeing advice. The Barcelona Provincial Court dismissed one of the charges in 2024, maintaining that Negreira was not a public figure and hence bribery charges cannot be upheld. So why have the charges come back? Well, bitter rivals Real Madrid presented a hardly believable 50,000 pages worth of evidence to UEFA to reignite their disciplinary investigation into sports corruption charges. The criminal case against the same allegations also remains open in the Spanish courts, with hearings scheduled for November. The Negreira case adds to the financial mishaps that have plagued Barca under presidents Josep Bartomeu and Joan Laporta. And the new evidence submitted by Real Madrid has caused further divide, as evidenced by the backlash over Vinicius Jr’s red card in the first game after the international break. Current La Liga president Javier Tebas has become embroiled in the situation too, calling the campaign by Real Madrid TV Nazi-esque propaganda. Real Madrid has officially condemned the statement and demanded Tebas resign. While the Negreria case resembles the infamous Calciopoli scandal that saw Juventus relegated in 2006, it is much harder to prove, since there is no documentation of payments to match referees. If the court deems the payments to Negreira influenced refereeing in Barca’s favour, Barca could also be facing a nullification of trophies in the seasons the club was allegedly favoured, a docking of points which could result in relegation, and significant fines. RONALDO’S EGOTISTICAL MESS In the middle of all this, even CR7 and his ego seem like small fish. Cristiano Ronaldo walked out of a training session and left the squad after an altercation with new Portuguese coach Jorge Jesus over not being played in a match. A 1,700-word Instagram post ensued from Ronaldo, before he was suspended for 30 days by the Portuguese FA. People may call it pettiness at 41 years of age, but the real fight for survival is elsewhere. The writer is a sports enthusiast with a background in supply chain management. INFRASTRUCTURE: DERA ISMAIL KHAN’S SOLAR REVOLUTION. In May 2026, Islamabad-based vlogger Muhammad Mobeen filmed Dera Ismail Khan’s famous Chowgalla, the British-era town centre where four bazaars intersect, using a drone. The video glides over the crowded bazaars in the heart of Dera Ismail Khan before pulling back to reveal buildings packed tightly together. As the camera pulls back, rooftops fill the frame, covered not in the usual clutter of water tanks and laundry lines but in sleek black and blue solar panels, stretching as far as the eye can see. The video has garnered roughly a million views and more than 25,000 likes on TikTok alone. Its popularity has spawned a host of copycat videos, with some content creators dubbing the city “Solar Ismail Khan.” The city’s urban area covers approximately 40 square kilometres and has a population of roughly 210,000, according to the 2023 census. Beyond the spectacle of thousands of solar panels covering the city’s rooftops, Dera Ismail Khan’s solar transition is beginning to reshape the local economy. It is creating new opportunities while making some traditional trades less viable in this dusty, conflict-affected city in southern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, roughly 300 kilometres from Peshawar. From specialised solar markets to farmers abandoning diesel-powered irrigation, an unreliable grid is driving a new economy in Dera Ismail Khan — but not everyone can afford to join it A SOLAR BOOM Over the past few years, three specialised solar markets have emerged in the city, at Khushal Market, Bannu Adda and Tank Road. Circular Road alone has up to 70 shops dealing exclusively in solar equipment, serving as a major distribution hub for neighbouring Tank, and Upper and Lower South Waziristan. The boom has extended beyond retail, creating work in solar installation, electrical wiring and the supply and maintenance of batteries, tube wells and related equipment. Muhammad Saeed, a local solar appliances dealer, says that, by his estimates, the majority of households in the city have adopted solar power. “Those who installed solar [systems] earlier are now upgrading to lithium batteries as prices fall,” says Saeed. The solar transition has also created ancillary jobs in supply chains and logistics, as well as work for solar-panel cleaners and wiring technicians. At the same time, traditional electricians are seeing a decline in conventional electrical-appliances repairs. “If consumers use solar energy instead of grid electricity, there is less need for repairs,” electrician Muhammad Naveed tells Eos. To supplement his income, Naveed now also takes on jobs involving solar systems, including for tube wells, alongside specialised wiring work. THE PRICE OF POWER Saeed and other solar traders say the city’s crippling, year-round power outages are the biggest driver of the transition. Data from the Peshawar Electric Supply Company (Pesco) show that 43 of the city’s 83 electricity feeders record line losses of at least 80 per cent. Pesco also identifies widespread electricity theft as a problem in the area. A spokesperson for the power utility tells Eos that such areas may face outages lasting 16 to 18 hours a day. Rising temperatures add to the pressure on residents. During summer, daytime temperatures in Dera Ismail Khan frequently reach 40–45 degrees Celsius, adding to the incentive to seek alternatives. Dera Ismail Khan’s solar boom is part of a wider shift across Pakistan, driven in part by falling prices for Chinese-made panels and rising electricity tariffs over the past four years. A report by the UK-based energy think tank Ember, titled The Solarisation of Pakistan’s Energy Economy, estimates that Pakistan’s solar power generation rose by 21 terawatt-hours (TWh) in just two years, taking the total increase to 33 TWh. Distributed solar accounted for 28 per cent of Pakistan’s electricity generation in FY25, up from 10 per cent in FY23, the report says. Eight 585-watt panel solar systems have a combined rated capacity of 4.68 kilowatts (kW). According to local traders, a system of this size can power an air conditioner, refrigerator, lights and fans, with battery storage providing back-up when solar generation is insufficient. According to solar trader Ali Jan, an individual panel that sold for Rs75,000 not long ago now costs roughly Rs16,000, following a global glut that drove down solar-panel prices. The price per watt has fallen from Rs128 to around Rs28, he says. The cost of an eight-panel set-up fell to around Rs220,000, says Jan, adding that households could recoup the investment within one to two years through savings on electricity. The imposition of general sales tax on solar imports last year, along with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, has pushed prices back up, Naveed explains. “Today, solar panels sell for up to 32 rupees per watt in Dera Ismail Khan, bringing the cost of an eight-panel installation to approximately 280,000 rupees,” he says. THE UNEVEN DIVIDENDS Dr Aijaz Ahmed has had small solar panels installed at his home and clinic for more than a decade. “In most months, I do not have to pay for electricity,” he tells Eos. “At the clinic, too, the electricity bill is a fraction of what it used to be,” he says. The savings extend beyond households. Small industries and commercial enterprises, facing high grid-electricity tariffs and rising fuel costs, have also embraced solar power. One businessman estimates that running a stone-crushing plant on a diesel generator costs up to Rs1.8 million a month. Converting it to solar would require an initial investment of around Rs10.5 million, he says, which could be recovered in just under three years. Commercial markets and wedding halls are also installing solar systems, with some businesses seeking to reduce or eliminate their dependence on grid electricity. Farmers are following a similar trend. A solar-powered irrigation system, capable of serving 10 acres of farmland, now costs around Rs9 million, according to Ali Jan. Rising fuel costs are also encouraging farmers to switch to solar-powered tube wells, reducing their dependence on diesel-powered irrigation. Local solar-equipment prices are now closely tied to those in Karachi. Dealers say that a one-rupee-per-watt increase in Karachi is quickly reflected in local prices. Freight charges from Karachi to Dera Ismail Khan have also risen, from around Rs270,000 to Rs350,000 per container since the conflict involving Iran began. The city’s newer commercial markets, including Gomal, Khyber, Anarkali, Mian Commercial and Gulf Plaza, also face the challenge of keeping shops lit and cooled. Their enclosed spaces and cooling requirements make reliable electricity particularly important. Rising electricity tariffs and fuel costs have made diesel generators increasingly expensive to operate, encouraging businesses to invest in solar power. WHO GETS LEFT BEHIND But the transition has also created a divide between those who can afford solar installations and those who cannot. While households and businesses with sufficient resources can reduce their dependence on an unreliable grid, poorer residents remain reliant on electricity they may struggle to afford — or continue to endure long power outages. Amir Khan, a social worker who runs the “Amir Bhai” Facebook page to help families in need, says poor single women are particularly disadvantaged when it comes to accessing solar power. Khan, who has more than 500,000 Facebook followers, began financing his welfare work himself in 2018. He says he now receives numerous requests from low-income families seeking help with solar installations. The solar panels that now dominate Dera Ismail Khan’s rooftops tell only part of the story. Beneath them, new businesses are emerging and old trades are adapting, while families unable to afford the transition remain dependent on an unreliable grid. In a city increasingly known as “Solar Ismail Khan”, access to electricity is becoming a question not just of supply, but of purchasing power. The writer is a Peshawar-based reporter for Dawn, with over 15 years of experience covering governance, climate and the economy in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
