US costs of Iran war rise to over $47bn, according to Pentagon estimate. The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran , more than 25 per cent higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters . The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly. The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict. More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “ platform losses ,” which include the loss of aircraft, including many drones lost during the war. Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time. Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful. But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible. Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so. The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war. While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

'Conscience does not permit': LHC's Justice Kayani resigns, cites 'executive's growing control' over judiciary. LAHORE: Lahore High Court’s (LHC) Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani resigned on Wednesday, citing personal reasons, including health concerns following a recent surgery, and “reasons of conscience”. In his resignation letter to the president of Pakistan, a copy of which is available with Dawn , Justice Kayani said it had been a privilege for him to serve at the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and LHC. “These years of judicial service remain among the most meaningful and fulfilling of my life. During my tenure, I have disposed of more than 23,000 cases of various categories, endeavouring always to uphold the Constitution, safeguard fundamental rights, and administer justice without fear or favour,” he continued. However, he added, “in my considered view, the changes introduced through the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments have compromised the independence and institutional integrity of the high courts”. “I have witnessed what I regard as the executive’s growing control over judicial institutions, extending to the appointment and transfer of judges. Such interference has, in my assessment, seriously eroded public confidence in judicial independence and the fairness of the judicial process.” Justice Kayani stated that of particular concern was the plight of the ordinary litigant, “who is the principal stakeholder in the justice system, yet whose suffering continues to deepen”. The needs of those seeking justice had too often been neglected, while other actors had become the “beneficiaries of a system intended to serve them”, he said. “In these circumstances, my conscience does not permit me to continue on the bench. This is a painful decision, but it reflects my conviction that judicial office must remain inseparable from independence, fidelity to the Constitution, and the protection of human dignity. “I, therefore, consider that the time has come for me to lay down my robes and return to legal practice, through which I intend to continue serving the people, protecting their rights, and promoting legal awareness,” he added. The judge ended his letter expressing gratitude to “my teachers, fellow judges and family members for their guidance and steadfast support, including during the deliberations that led to this decision”. His resignation has come years before the date of his retirement — Feb 10, 2032. He hails from Islamabad and was serving at the IHC before his transfer to the LHC in April. He was assigned to the LHC’s principal seat in Lahore. Despite being a senior judge of the LHC, he was not assigned to any division bench. Justice Kayani previously served as the senior puisne judge of the IHC and was expecting to be elevated to the post of the high court’s chief justice. However, the transfer of incumbent IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar from the LHC, along with two other judges from the Sindh and Balochistan high courts, prompted him to challenge the inter-high court transfers. The Supreme Court’s constitutional bench upheld the transfers to the IHC, including that of Justice Dogar. The decision, however, triggered a broader legal battle. Justice Kayani and other senior IHC judges approached the Supreme Court to challenge the administrative powers exercised by Chief Justice Dogar. They alleged that the office had been turned into a “monocracy” and that judges could be excluded from the roster at will. Following his own transfer to the LHC, Justice Kayani lost his seniority and was placed 12th on the high court’s seniority list. His resignation came days after he returned to the twin cities to preside over a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry following a reshuffle at the high court. The new duty roster assigned him only to a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry despite his previous position as the IHC’s senior puisne judge. Justice Kayani was also one of the six IHC judges who had accused the country’s intelligence apparatus of interference in judicial affairs, including attempts to pressure judges through abduction and torture of their relatives and secret surveillance inside their homes in a startling letter to the Supreme Judicial Council (SJC) members in March 2024. Education and career According to information available on the LHC’s website, Justice Kayani completed his early education at FG Boys High School in Islamabad and pursued higher education at FG College for Men. He graduated in 1989. The judge earned his LLB from the University of Punjab in 1994, followed by an MA degree in Political Science in 1996, an LLM from Karachi University in 2003 and a MSc in Pakistan Studies in 2005. He also has postgraduate diploma in human rights from Peshawar University in collaboration with the Norwegian Institute of Human Rights, Oslo University. Justice Kayani was enrolled as an advocate of the district courts in 1995 and ascended to the high court in 1997 and the Supreme Court in 2009. He was appointed as an IHC judge on Dec 23, 2015 and transferred to the LHC on April 29 this year. The judge also served as the joint secretary of the Islamabad District Bar Association from 1998 to 1999, general secretary of the Islamabad District Bar Association from 2002 to 2003 and the president of the Islamabad High Court Bar Association from 2013 to 2014. “He has presided over significant cases, particularly those related to enforced disappearances. Justice Kayani has advocated for legislative reforms, including proposing strict penalties for enforced disappearances, reflecting his commitment to justice and the rule of law,” the website says.

AI’s brain & muscle. ARTIFICIAL intelligence is usually presented as weightless, almost entirely digital. We ask it to write, calculate, translate or create an image, and the response appears instantly. Yet every answer depends on a substantial physical system. This comprises data centres, specialised processors, cooling equipment etc. In reality AI has both ‘brain’ and ‘muscle’. Algorithms, software, researchers, engineers and companies comprise its brain. Its muscle consists of electricity, computing infrastructure, minerals, manufacturing capacity and reliable networks. The first phase of global AI competition focused mainly on the brain. As AI becomes more widely used, the muscle is becoming impossible to ignore. The International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from data centres to more than double by 2030, with AI a major driver. The challenge is not simply producing more power. It is producing reliable electricity supply and expanded transmission networks to accommodate the needs of large data centres. Oil and gas reserves beneath the ground are not the same as electricity delivered to a data centre. Resources become strategic only when they can be converted into dependable infrastructure. The physical foundations of AI also include copper, aluminium, silicon, and rare-earth materials. Advanced semiconductor technologies depend on specialised materials, while mining and refining remain concentrated in a limited number of countries. The digital economy has not escaped geography! An algorithm can cross a border in milliseconds, but a power plant, mine or factory cannot. This creates a new geopolitical equation. Countries with the strongest AI research and software ecosystems may still depend on others for energy, minerals and manufacturing. Resource-rich countries, meanwhile, may possess the muscle of the AI economy without the universities, capital, software and semiconductor capabilities needed to turn it into computing power. The long-term advantage may belong to countries that can connect the two. The digital economy has not escaped geography. Pakistan illustrates this challenge clearly. It is not currently a leading frontier-AI power and faces serious constraints in reliable electricity, advanced computing, research funding etc. Yet it has a large young population, growing software and IT-services sectors, universities, engineering talent, hydropower and renewable-energy potential, and significant mineral resources. The strategic challenge is therefore not simply to acquire more resources or develop more algorithms, but to connect the country’s physical assets with its scientific and technological capabilities. That would require moving beyond traditional models of exporting raw materials and low-value services. An AI-era strategy would use reliable energy, connectivity and mineral resources to support data centres, cloud services, local research, advanced applications and value-added manufacturing. AI could strengthen sectors such as agriculture, textiles, logistics, mining, health, education and public administration. In this model, AI becomes an industrial multiplier rather than merely another software sector. Resource wealth alone, however, guarantees neither technological independence nor prosperity. Natural resources cannot substitute for universities, skilled workers, capital, innovation and capable institutions. The relationship between AI’s brain and muscle is better understood as multiplication rather than addition. A country with excellent algorithms but unreliable power will struggle to scale, while a country with abundant energy but weak research capacity may remain a commodity supplier. The lesson extends beyond Pakistan. Countries such as the United States have ex­­traordinary stren­gths in research, capital, technology companies and advanced computing. China combines rapidly advancing AI with industrial scale and manufacturing capacity. Gulf countries possess energy and capital, while Australia and Canada have substantial mineral and energy advantages. None controls every part of the AI system. Interdependence will remain unavoidable, but countries that connect more stages, from energy and minerals to computing and applications, will have greater strategic influence. For Pakistan and other natural resource-rich countries, the message is immediate. An AI strategy cannot stop at applications, start-ups or policy statements . It must also address reliable electricity, data-centre infrastructure, digital skills, research institutions, mineral value addition and industrial capacity. The next phase of the AI race will not be decided solely by who builds the smartest models. It will also be decided by who can power them, supply them and apply them productively. AI has a brain. But without muscle, even the most brilliant brain cannot move. The writer is an educationist. Published in Dawn, October 28th, 2026

Imaan, Hadi allege security breach case 'nothing more than harassment' for their human rights work. Human rights lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, have alleged that the case against them pertaining to a security breach was “nothing more than harassment” for their legal and human rights work, falling under the broader pattern of targeting through “reprisals”. On Tuesday, the case concluded at Adiala Jail, with the anti-terrorism court (ATC) reserving its verdict. Both accused recorded their statements under Section 342 (power to examine the accused) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, while final arguments by the state counsel also concluded during the proceedings. Imaan and Hadi are facing a jail trial in a 2024 case on the alleged disruption of an international cricket team’s security route and incitement to public unrest. The couple, accused of removing barriers from the route, were indicted on Oct 7. “The evidence produced during this trial is not against us, but in fact a charge sheet against (prosecution witnesses)/police officials and the state,” Imaan and Hadi said in their separate similar recorded statements available with Dawn . They claimed that the prosecution witnesses were “part and parcel” of the state machinery that had allegedly targeted them for their human rights work and provision of pro bono legal assistance and services to the marginalised and oppressed communities, including street vendors and victims of false blasphemy allegations and enforced disappearances. “I am a prisoner of conscience who has been at the receiving end of state persecution,” the statements by the lawyer couple read. Imaan pointed out that the entire jail trial had been challenged by the couple in the Islamabad High Court (IHC) as well as the Supreme Court (SC). Further, the trial was conducted with Imaan and her husband being presented in a cage, preventing effective communication with their counsel or the court, she said. “From day one, our constitutional rights to fair trial, due process and basic human dignity have been infringed,” she stated. On the charges against the two of removing security barriers placed in connection with the movement of an international cricket team at Zarai Taraqiati Bank Limited on Faisal Avenue on Oct 25, 2024, Imaan stated she and her husband were on their way to the court when the police told them that the route had been temporarily closed as an alternative route for the cricket team. At this, Imaan said that she enquired whether the police officials had a copy of the magistrate’s order for closure, which the police did not have. She also pointed out that such an order was yet to be produced by the prosecution in the trial. Imaan denied the prosecution testimonies, saying they were “false, fabricated and contradictory” to the video footage of the incident. She further held that the video had also confirmed that one of the police officials threw a barrier at her lower abdomen, due to which she fell to the ground. “The timing and mode and manner (including both jail trial in a cage and speed of instant proceedings) of the trial reflect the objective to keep us behind bars at all costs,” Imaan claimed. She further alleged that prosecution witnesses had been directed by “higher-ups/senior officers to falsely depose against us to punish for our human rights work”. She also noted that the couple had been incarcerated for over nine months and handed 17-year sentences a day after their arrest on Jan 23. “We are being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression and injustice,” Imaan stated. The lawyer further highlighted that the two had spent the third year of their marriage in jail and thus “suffered painful separation from one another” very early on. “We have not done so for any personal gain; in fact, we have endured only hardship for our work (and) activism,” she said. “But we surrender ourselves before the ultimate court where we all must return one day, where all will be held accountable for what they have done.” Meanwhile, Hadi, in his recorded statement available with Dawn, said: “I am being punished for not only supporting my wife’s work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together.” He added: “It is deeply painful for me that while my work on human rights has received recognition abroad, even today, my family and I continue to suffer reprisals for the same in my home country.” On Monday, the couple approached the SC to challenge the IHC’s Oct 19 order refusing to stay the trial in the case. The IHC had heard their appeals last week against an Oct 10 ATC order dismissing petitions challenging the framing of charges and the inclusion of terrorism-related provisions. The high court issued notices and said it would decide how to proceed after receiving responses from the parties. Jailed, sentenced, re-arrested The couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the IHC and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act in the controversial social media posts case. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the SC suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the IHC’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with the security breach case. The case was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio.

Govt considering creation of 2 regulatory authorities for construction industry, 3-year liability period for projects. ISLAMABAD: The government is considering establishing up to two regulatory authorities for the construction industry and a three-year defect liability period for major construction projects in the country. Private sector figures in construction and the government, however, differ over the financial size for the application of a defect liability period, with the construction industry seeking a minimum threshold of Rs20 billion and the government pushing for lower amounts. These issues were discussed at an exploratory meeting, chaired by Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Cheema, on introducing reforms for the country’s construction sector, improving project delivery and addressing key issues faced by the industry. Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani, Secretary Housing retired captain Muhammad Mahmood and other senior officials also attended the meeting. The meeting discussed the proposed Construction Industry Development Authority (CIDA) Bill, with Cheema stressing that it required detailed consideration, including whether to establish a single body for the construction sector or two separate entities — one to regulate the sector and another to promote the construction industry and handle related matters. The participants decided to continue engagements with stakeholders, including the relevant agencies led by Kayani and representatives of the Constructors Association of Pakistan (CAP), and to fine-tune the proposed institutional structure. Retention money deposited by contractors during the defect liability period was also discussed, with a proposal considered to place these funds in accounts that earn a return, with the principal amount and interest paid back to contractors after the stipulated period. Cheema called for further consultation to develop a workable mechanism. Additionally, the meeting considered applying the existing Dispute Avoidance and Adjudication Board (DAAB) mechanism to government projects. DAAB would monitor project implementation and help prevent or resolve disputes as they arise, while CAP proposed applying the mechanism to projects valued at Rs20bn and above. However, Cheema called for the proposed threshold to be lowered and further consultation among relevant stakeholders to determine an appropriate limit. The forthcoming framework for the construction sector will also draw on the rules and standards of the International Federation of Consulting Engineers (FIDIC). Cheema underscored the importance of using these international standards as a key reference. The meeting also directed the Pakistan Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (PPRA) to begin work on introducing a defect liability period for major projects of at least three years or more, with the measure to be extended to smaller projects in phases. In August, it emerged that the government was contemplating a comprehensive package to invigorate the construction industry, aiming to simplify regulations, attract investment, and bolster institutional support. The package envisaged a series of measures, including the establishment of a Construction Industry Development Board (CIDB), the evaluation of a dedicated Construction Development Bank (CDB), the rationalisation of import and export policies, and targeted tax reforms for the construction sector.

ECP orders immediate local body polls in KP districts demarcated, sans those under ARDC. ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Wednesday ordered local government (LG) elections to be held immediately in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa districts where delimitation had been completed, excluding those included in the 12 districts with special emergency measures. A day earlier, the ECP had reserved the verdict after hearing the provincial government’s request to defer local government elections, citing law and order , the imposition of emergency and deployment of troops under Article 245. The federal government on Oct 11 imposed emergency in KP and placed the province under governor’s rule, taking note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. In its order, issued on Wednesday and seen by Dawn , the ECP directed its office to submit the election programme for its approval in respect of districts where the delimitation process had been completed. The bench headed by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Sikandar Sultan Raja and comprising members Nisar Ahmed Durrani, Shah Muhammad Jatoi, Babar Hassan Bharwana and retired Justice Ikramullah Khan heard the case. The electoral watchdog issued orders for KP districts, excluding 12 which were deemed to face intense security challenges and an Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) was formed to oversee them under emergency measures. In its order, the ECP directed its office to “submit the election programme for the commission’s approval in respect of districts in which the delimitation process has been completed”, excluding Bannu, Mohmand, Orakzai, Lakki Marwat and North Waziristan specified in the federal government’s order dated Oct 11. The ECP also sought the issuance of the delimitation schedules for the remaining districts, excluding Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Bajaur, Khyber, Kurram, Lower South Waziristan and Upper South Waziristan. It issued the directives under Articles 218(3) (Election Commission), 140A(2) (local government), 219(d) (duties of ECP), 220 (executive authorities to assist ECP) and 222 (electoral laws) of the Constitution, read with Sections 219 (ECP to conduct elections) and 221 (delimitation of LG constituencies) of the Elections Act 2017, and “all other enabling provisions of law”. The order further directed the ECP’s office to adjust and determine the number of village councils/neighbourhood councils and category-wise reserved seats in respect of each tehsil council in seven districts, ie, Karak, Hangu, Swat, Bar Swat, Battagram, Paharpur and Allai as per current revenue limits in accordance with separate order of the commission of even date to ensure timely conduct of LG elections and delimitation in the districts other than designated districts. The local government elections in KP have remained pending since the terms of existing local bodies expired — the first phase in March 2026 and the second phase in June 2026. In July this year, the KP government had assured the ECP of “all possible support” in holding LG polls where delimitation was complete. Later, the ECP had opposed a key amendment in KP’s local government law regarding the population of village and neighbourhood councils, terming it a delaying tactic.

Filing your tax return on IRIS: A step-by-step guide for the salaried individual. Most of us feel a small knot in the stomach when someone mentions a “tax return”. We picture stacks of paper, a consultant’s fee, and a long queue at a tax office. The good news is that none of that is needed any more. If you are a salaried person, you can file your return yourself, from home, on the Federal Board of Revenue’s (FBR) online portal, IRIS. It is free and with your papers in hand it usually takes under an hour. This guide walks you through it, one click at a time. For Tax Year 2026, the last date to file is Oct 31. Why should I bother filing at all? Think of your tax return as the yearly hisaab (account) you settle at your neighbourhood shop. All year, your employer has been paying tax on your behalf every month, just like items going onto a shop’s khata (record). The return is the day you sit down with the shopkeeper, match the totals and sign off. If the shop owes you, you get it back. If you owe a little, you clear it. Either way, the book is closed and you walk away with a clean slate. Once your hisaab is settled, your name goes onto the FBR’s “Active Taxpayers List” (ATL). That is what people mean when they say someone is a “filer”. Being a filer matters in everyday life. Non-filers pay noticeably higher tax on things like bank transactions, buying a car or property, and other big-ticket dealings. And being late has become expensive. From this year, an individual who misses the deadline must pay a surcharge of Rs 25,000 to get back onto the ATL. Until last year it was Rs 1,000. Do I need to file? You should file if any of these apply to you for the year July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026: Your salary was more than Rs 600,000 for the year (Rs 50,000 a month). You own a car of 1000cc or above, or own property. You earned rent, profit on savings, dividends or business income. You want to enjoy filer rates on banking, property or vehicle deals. A common misunderstanding that comes up every tax season is the following: “My employer already cuts tax from my salary, so I’m covered.” You are not. Your employer pays the tax, but only you can file the return. Without it, you will not appear on the ATL. A simple rule of thumb: if in doubt, file. Even if you owe nothing, a return showing zero tax still makes you a filer. What does ‘Tax Year 2026’ mean? This one confuses almost everyone. Tax Year 2026 simply means the income you earned from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026. It is named after the year in which it ends. So the return you are filing now, in October 2026, is for the salary you received over the last financial year. What do I need before I start? Keep these ready before you open the website. IRIS can be slow during the filing season, so the less you have to hunt for midway, the better. Your Computerised National Identity Card (CNIC) A mobile number registered in your own name, and an email address you can open. Your salary certificate (also called the annual tax deduction certificate) from your employer. It shows your total salary and the total tax deducted for the year. Ask your HR or accounts department. Tax deducted on other things, such as your mobile phone bills, electricity bills, car token tax, and profit on bank savings. Your bank can give you a withholding tax certificate. A list of what you own and what you owe on June 30, 2026: property, car, cash at home, bank balances, gold, any loans. Rough figures for your household expenses for the year: rent, utilities, school fees, travel and so on. Last year’s return, if you filed one. It makes the wealth statement much easier. Tip: write all these figures down in a notebook or a simple spreadsheet first. Typing them into IRIS from a ready sheet is quick and stress-free. Step 1: How do I register if this is my first time? If you have filed before, skip to Step 2. Go to iris.fbr.gov.pk . Click “Registration for Unregistered Person”. Enter your CNIC (without dashes), your name, your mobile number and your email address. Use a SIM that is registered against your own CNIC; shared or relatives’ numbers are a common cause of trouble. FBR will send you two one-time codes: one by SMS and one by email. Enter both. You will then receive your login password, again by SMS and email. Log in using your CNIC as the user name. You will be asked to fill a short registration form (called Form 181) with your address and source of income. If you are salaried, you will need your employer’s name and National Tax Number (NTN), which Human Resources can give you. Submit it. Once accepted, your CNIC number becomes your NTN number. Step 2: How do I open the return form? Log in at iris.fbr.gov.pk with your CNIC and password. From the top menu, click “Declaration”, then choose the income tax return. Select the period 2026. If most of your income comes from salary (more than half), choose Form 114(I). This is the simplified return made for salaried people, and it is by far the easiest. Your personal details will already be filled in from your registration. Just check them. Step 3: How do I enter my salary? Take out your salary certificate. You need two numbers from it: Total salary for the year. Total tax deducted by your employer. Enter them in the salary section exactly as they appear. Do not round off and do not estimate. The figures should match what your employer has reported to FBR. Step 4: How do I claim the tax I have already paid elsewhere? Throughout the year, small amounts of tax were also taken from you in other places. These are called “withholding taxes” and many of them can be “adjusted”, meaning they count towards your total bill. Common ones include tax on: mobile phone bills electricity bills car token tax profit on bank savings IRIS often fills some of these in automatically. Check each figure against your bills and certificates, and add anything that is missing. Going back to our shop: this is like reminding the shopkeeper of the payments you already made on the side. They belong in the hisaab . Step 5: What is the wealth statement and how do I fill it? The wealth statement is a snapshot of what you owned and what you owed on 30 June 2026. You list your: Assets: house or plot, car, bank balances, cash in hand, gold and jewellery, investments. Liabilities: home loan, car loan, money borrowed from someone. Personal expenses for the year: rent, utilities, school fees, travel, and so on. Here is the part that confuses people. IRIS checks that your story adds up. What you owned last year + what you earned this year − what you spent = what you own this year. If these do not match, IRIS shows an “unreconciled amount”. It must come to zero before you can submit. This is the shopkeeper’s khata again. The opening balance, plus what came in, minus what went out, must equal the closing balance. If it does not, usually an expense or an asset is missing or mistyped. Go back, check your figures, and adjust honestly. Be truthful here. Penalties for hiding assets or giving misleading information have been raised sharply this year. Declaring what you own is your protection, not a risk. Step 6: How do I know if I owe anything? Click “Calculate”. IRIS will work out your tax and compare it with what has already been paid. You will see one of three results: Zero: your employer has paid exactly the right amount. This is the most common outcome for salaried people. Refundable: you have paid more than you owed. You may claim this back. Payable: you owe a little more. For a sense of scale, here is roughly what a salaried person owes for Tax Year 2026: Monthly salary Yearly salary Yearly tax Rs 50,000 Rs 600,000 Nil Rs 100,000 Rs 1,200,000 Rs 6,000 Rs 200,000 Rs 2,400,000 Rs 162,000 If your employer has been deducting tax properly, most of this will already be paid. Step 7: How do I pay if there is a balance? In IRIS, create a payment slip for income tax. This generates a PSID, a payment slip ID number. Pay that PSID through your bank’s mobile app, internet banking or at a branch. Once paid, you get a CPR (Computerised Payment Receipt) number. Enter the CPR number in your return so IRIS knows the tax has been paid. Step 8: How do I submit? Check the unreconciled amount once more. It must be zero. Click “Submit”. Enter the PIN you created when you first registered. IRIS will issue an acknowledgement slip. Download it and keep it safe, along with a copy of your return. This is your proof of filing. Congratulations. Your hisaab is closed for the year. Step 9: How do I check that I am now a filer? Once the ATL is updated, you can check your status in two easy ways: By SMS: type ATL, a space, then your 13-digit CNIC, and send it to 9966. Online: search your CNIC on the ATL section of FBR’s website. What if IRIS is slow or keeps giving errors? You will not be alone. IRIS has been sluggish this season, especially close to the deadline. File early. Do not wait for the final day. Try during quiet hours, early morning or late at night. Click “Save” often. The auto-save feature has been removed this year, so an unsaved page can be lost. Keep your figures on paper or in a spreadsheet, so re-entering them is quick if something goes wrong. If an error message makes no sense, take a screenshot and contact the FBR’s helpline or a tax practitioner. Myths vs reality Myth: “My employer deducts tax, so I don’t need to file.” Reality: Your employer pays the tax. Only you can file the return. Myth: “My income is too low to bother.” Reality: Filing a return showing zero tax still makes you a filer, and that saves you money elsewhere. Myth: “If I declare my car or plot, I’ll get a notice.” Reality: It is hiding assets that gets you into trouble, and penalties for that have gone up. Myth: “I need to pay a consultant.” Reality: Not for a simple salaried return. This guide is all you need. When should I get professional help? You can do a simple salaried return yourself. Consider a tax practitioner if you have: A business or freelance income More than one property or rental income Sold property or shares during the year Income or assets abroad The bottom line Filing your return is not a favour to the government. It is a small, once-a-year chore that keeps your own finances clean and saves you real money on the big purchases of life: a car, a home, your children’s future. Gather your papers, set aside an evening, and settle your hisaab . Do it before Oct 31, and do it once properly. Next year, it will take you half the time. Dates and rules quoted are as announced by FBR at the time of writing. Please check iris.fbr.gov.pk or FBR’s announcements for any further changes before you file.

How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iranians commute past a billboard depicting slain Lebanese Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran on September 27, 2026. ATTA KENARE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 16 October 2026 12 minutes How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” Three years of hostilities have transformed Tehran’s network of allies in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic is now relying more heavily on itself, while adapting its relationships with partners whose diminished military utility has not necessarily reduced its commitment to their protection. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Hamidreza Azizi Senior Analyst, Iran https://x.com/HamidRezaAz Related Tags Iran Israel/Palestine Lebanon Syria Developments since 7 October 2023, when Hamas staged its deadly attacks on southern Israel, have transformed Iran’s network of state and non-state allies in the Middle East, as well as their role in Tehran’s military planning and deterrence posture. The weakening of Hamas and Hizbollah at Israel’s hands in the last three years, the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria in December 2024 and, above all, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February have altered the vectors of Iranian influence. Together, these events have exposed the limits of an Iranian strategy that had relied chiefly on regional partners to deter adversaries and keep any armed confrontation away from Iran itself. Instead, Tehran now places greater weight on capabilities under its direct control: missiles, drones and the ability to obstruct traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. This evolution does not mean that the “ axis of resistance ”, as Iran calls its collection of allies, has lost all relevance. Rather, it means that axis members are now assuming different functions and that Tehran is approaching them differently. Yemen’s Houthis have gained particularly significant strategic value for Iran because their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping complements Tehran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. In Iraq, major Shiite factions also remain important political partners, even as Tehran increasingly turns to smaller armed groups to conduct military operations. Overall, the result is a more fragmented network in which heightened local autonomy among Iran’s non-state partners coexists with tighter Iranian control of select cells and smaller armed organisations. Nor is a weaker “axis of resistance” necessarily synonymous with diminished Iranian commitment to its partners. Hizbollah’s lesser contribution to Iranian deterrence, for example, has not reduced Tehran’s determination to protect the Lebanese Shiite movement. To the contrary, Iran has shown itself more willing to use force in Hizbollah’s defence; it also has conditioned reaching a deal terminating its hostilities with the United States on an end to Israel’s campaign in Lebanon. In other terms, Iran still may be drawn into conflicts on its regional partners’ behalf, even as they have become less capable of shielding it from attack. From the Levant to Maritime Chokepoints Prior to October 2023, Iran’s Middle East strategy centred on the Levant . Syria under Assad’s rule was the linchpin, the only Arab state allied with Iran, which provided it with substantial benefits: a land corridor linking Iran and its Iraqi Shiite partners to Hizbollah; proximity to Israel’s borders; and a logistical hub that enabled Tehran to project its influence to the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. In June 2024, Yahya Rahim Safavi , a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who was then military adviser to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, likened Iran’s reach through the axis to that of the ancient Persian empire under Cyrus and Xerxes. The advantages of alliance with Assad explain why, over a decade of civil war in Syria, Tehran defended his regime at significant cost. Hizbollah fighters also helped the regime a great deal, battling both its domestic opponents and ISIS. Hizbollah was useful in another important way, offering Tehran a means of threatening Israel from adjacent territory, thus ostensibly deterring it from direct strikes on Iran itself. If Assad’s Syria was a linchpin of the Islamic Republic’s Middle East strategy, the Shiite movement in Lebanon was a principal engine. [Assad’s fall] deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. This arrangement has suffered severe damage since October 2023 , when Hamas – apparently taking even Iran’s leadership by surprise – attacked Israel. The Gaza campaign that Israel launched in response dealt the axis a first blow, although Iran’s relationship with the Palestinian group has never been on par with those it has enjoyed with its other affiliates. Assad’s fall – indirectly part of the chain of events triggered by the Hamas attacks – was far more consequential. It deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. After Hizbollah entered the post-2023 fray, Israeli counter-attacks also inflicted substantial losses on the Lebanese movement’s leadership and military assets, while causing significant death, destruction and displacement in the country. As a result, other Lebanese factions began issuing more urgent calls on Hizbollah to disarm. The setbacks reinforced one another: rebuilding a degraded Hizbollah was a far more daunting task without the Syrian channel that had previously sustained it. These losses notwithstanding, Tehran has yet to forsake the Levant. Hizbollah still has a strong, institutionalised relationship with Iran, significant political weight in Lebanon and the capacity to regroup, at least in part. The Israeli incursions into southern Syria following the Assad regime’s demise may also have benefits for Iran. The Islamic Republic may be banking on local resistance to Israel eventually creating openings for renewed Iranian influence in Syria, though this prospect remains uncertain. For now, Iran has turned its attention to an arena closer to its borders where it retains heftier clout. On 8 June, Esmail Qaani , commander ofthe Revolutionary Guards’ overseas operations arm, the Qods Force, described an emerging “security belt” stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea. When compared to Safavi’s formulation two years prior, the phrase captures a shift in emphasis from the Levant to the maritime routes linking the Gulf to the western Indian Ocean, a theatre in which Iran’s sway comes more directly from its own place on the map. The Islamic Republic requires neither an allied state nor a non-state partner to project power in the Strait of Hormuz; it can station missiles and drones nearby or even deep inland to threaten naval or commercial vessels in these waters. Tehran’s influence over maritime routes upon which states near and far depend for trade in oil, gas and other vital commodities is boosted by its partnership with the Houthis, who can fire at ships passing in either direction through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Though it no longer serves as a land bridge for arms transfers to Syria and Lebanon, Iraq nonetheless plays an important part in this changing landscape. In particular, it is a locus for coordination between the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups , as well as between the Qods Force and Iraqi groups that have conducted attacks on Gulf Arab states. A More Fragmented Network The shift in Iran’s primary focus from the Levant to the seas has gone hand in hand with organisational changes. Under its late commander Qassem Soleimani, the Qods Force was the principal coordinator of “axis of resistance” activities. Since the U.S. killed Soleimani in January 2020, the Qods Force has not played the same role. Subsequent wars and leadership losses, both within the Revolutionary Guards and among its partners, further discombobulated command structures and impaired joint military operations. As a result, Iran has had to adapt its relationships with groups whose military capabilities and domestic constraints themselves have changed. It has increasingly been compelled to work through smaller groups or selected elements of established organisations. This trend has been most evident in Iraq. As the years passed after Saddam Hussein’s ouster, older Shiite political movements acquired key government positions and economic interests, thus becoming more beholden to popular constituencies. As a result, they are now more hesitant to engage in military action that risks provoking retaliation or eroding their standing. This reluctance was apparent early in the present U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, when several major Iraqi Shiite armed groups declined to mobilise on Tehran’s behalf. Iran had to rely on smaller, less prominent ones – drawn from the self-styled Islamic Resistance in Iraq – to come to its aid. Iraqi sources speak of a network of clandestine cells established by the Revolutionary Guards and operating outside established militias’ command structures that reportedly has been responsible for attacks on Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. These nimbler, smaller groups offer Tehran several advantages. They require fewer resources, they can conceal their affiliations and they can ignore the political constraints holding back their larger counterparts. Their greater ideological cohesion also arguably makes them easier for Tehran to direct. More institutionalised Iraqi Shiite groups remain important to Tehran, notwithstanding their reticence regarding military action in Iran’s defence. But their role has shifted: they are useful principally because they help Iran preserve influence in the country as well as the political space in which smaller armed groups are free to operate. Iran’s changing relationship with Hizbollah illustrates another type of adjustment to similar pressures. Though the movement retains a substantial organisation that helps Tehran sustain influence in Lebanon, Hizbollah’s military actions increasingly resemble those of a guerrilla group – quick-hitting raids that leave the group less vulnerable to Israeli airstrikes and intelligence penetration. Its use of first-person-view drones – drones using a live video feed from an onboard camera – to attack Israeli forces in southern Lebanon showcased the effectiveness of inexpensive technology, even as the movement has lost its more sophisticated capabilities. An Iranian expert with ties to both the Revolutionary Guards and Hizbollah told Crisis Group that Qods Force commanders have been directly involved in this revamping, including efforts to work through smaller units and help Hizbollah fighters adopt more agile tactics. Deterrence Moves Closer to Home, but the Axis Remains Important These changes reflect a broader reassessment of Iran’s deterrence posture. Its earlier approach heavily relied on the concept of “ forward defence ” ensured by regional partners, supplemented by the threat of direct retaliation from its own territory. The “axis of resistance” gave the Islamic Republic strategic depth , discouraging its adversaries from attacking it and keeping conflict distant from its borders. Only if that first layer of protection were to fail were Iranian missiles and drones to be used to shoot back. The past three years of war have starkly exposed the limits inherent in this arrangement. Iran’s regional network did not prevent direct attacks on the country – whether the major exchanges with Israel in 2024, the surprise Israeli attack in June 2025 or the more substantial confrontation with the U.S. and Israel beginning in February. As the deterrence value of axis partners dropped, Tehran was compelled to place greater weight on its own capabilities: missiles, drones and geographical leverage. If military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Yet, if military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Though the axis as a whole no longer serves as the primary foundation of Iran’s deterrence, decision-makers in Tehran believe that certain partners can play important roles in particular circumstances as they magnify Iran’s own capabilities and geographical leverage. Their experience during the present conflict with the U.S. has only bolstered this conviction. The Houthis have attained particular importance in the Islamic Republic’s thinking, which helps explain reports that Tehran has provided them with both guidance and military assistance. Tehran’s efforts in July to establish direct flights to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen illustrated the multidimensional nature of this support: the flights both challenged restrictions imposed by Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia on Houthi rule and reportedly carried Revolutionary Guards commanders, military advisers and missile- and drone-related equipment. Hizbollah, too, has retained its usefulness for Tehran. The movement attacked Israel following February’s U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, forcing Israel to contend with an additional front and placing further demands on its air defences. True, that supporting role was a far cry from the crucial deterrent function the movement was intended to play, a reflection of its diminished capabilities. Iranian officials have nevertheless continued to frame their confrontation with the U.S. and Israel as extending to Iran’s Middle East partners, Hizbollah in particular. In June, in a remarkable role reversal, Iran launched missiles at Israel in response to its campaign against Hizbollah, thereby marshalling its own forces in defence of its partner rather than the other way around. Moreover, it conditioned its acceptance of the (short-lived) 17 June memorandum of understanding halting hostilities with the U.S. on cessation of Israeli attacks in Lebanon: the opening clause explicitly included Lebanon in the ceasefire and affirmed Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel persisted with its offensive, however, including at Ali al-Taher , a strategic Hizbollah position in southern Lebanon where Israel besieged (and, in mid-September, demolished) an underground command and weapons complex. To Iranian officials, who had reportedly sent warnings that any such act would provoke a “forceful” response, the demolition was a reminder that Iranian threats of renewed missile attacks were an insufficient deterrent. Still, Iran’s stance showcased its commitment to axis members whose military utility has faded but not been erased. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. According to Iranian experts interviewed by Crisis Group, several members of the security establishment regard Hizbollah’s survival in particular as being closely tied to Iran’s own security, giving the relationship a significance that extends beyond the movement’s immediate military capabilities. This outlook has surfaced in public debates. In a January 2025 interview published by Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, former diplomat Hadi Seyyed Afghahi argued that pressure on militant groups in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen was aimed at “Iran and, more generally, the Shiites of the region”. Therefore, Tehran could not remain indifferent to these groups’ fate. Likewise, in December 2025, Ali Samadzadeh , an analyst with close ties to the regime, argued that Iran should be prepared to intervene militarily if Israel attacked Hizbollah, describing an assault on Lebanon as a prelude to renewed war with Iran. Defending regional partners, in this view, is part and parcel of protecting Iran itself. In short, where Tehran regards a partner as key to its own security, the fact that the partner has been weakened arguably – and perhaps paradoxically – provides Iran with added reason to intervene on its behalf. Efforts to curb Iranian influence by targeting allied groups may therefore draw Tehran into conflicts – a marked departure from the role these groups once played in shielding the Islamic Republic from direct involvement in hostilities. The extent of Iranian involvement is likely to depend on the particular relationship in question and the risks and costs inherent in intervention. But the bottom line is that its partners’ diminished military capabilities will not necessarily reduce Iran’s exposure to, or participation in, their respective conflicts. A Shifting Picture After three years of hostilities involving Iran’s partners and, since February, Iran itself, the “axis of resistance” is neither down nor out, but it is not what it once was, either in the function it serves or in Tehran’s relationship to its various members. The changes have been manifold. First, some of its members’ military capabilities have been significantly degraded. Secondly, direct confrontation with the U.S. and Israel has revealed the groups’ limited deterrent value and their inability to keep conflict away from Iranian territory. Finally, and partly as a result of their lessened status, they have come under growing domestic political, economic and security pressure, hindering their ability to directly participate in confrontations involving the Islamic Republic. These changes do not rule out these groups’ continued close operational ties to Tehran; nor do they mean an end to Iran’s commitment to their protection. But, together, they constrain the groups’ freedom of action. As a result, the focus of the Islamic Republic’s strategic doctrine has pivoted from allied non-state actors toward its own capabilities. This adjustment undoubtedly has preserved Iran’s ability to project power in its neighbourhood. But it does not come without serious risk, insofar as it has led Tehran to more directly bear the costs and dangers of confrontation. The Islamic Republic may well find ways to manage the consequences of its partners’ weakened clout by coming to their aid when they are endangered, giving them breathing space to regroup and using its own military assets to deter its foes, including by ensuring that others – notably Gulf Arab states – suffer the consequences of Middle East war. In so doing, Iran hopes to discourage future attacks. But this approach also risks deepening hostility among its neighbours, potentially encouraging closer security cooperation among Iran’s adversaries and heightening the very pressures Tehran seeks to reduce. Has the Israeli political “centre” shifted so much that even new leaders may not bring real change? In this online event, Crisis Group brought together leading Israeli political analysts to tackle this and other questions. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Israel/Palestine The Knesset elections on 27 October could be the most consequential in Israel’s short history. After four years of hard-right government under Benjamin Netanyahu, and three years of war on multiple fronts since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israelis head to the polls with starkly different hopes for their future. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the threshold needed to enter the 120-seat parliament. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Whichever bloc comes out on top, a question hangs over the vote: has the Israeli political “centre” shifted so much that even new leaders may not bring real change – at least, not on big issues that matter to the rest of the world, such as accommodating the 7.5 million Palestinians that live under Israeli rule? In this online event, Crisis Group brought together leading Israeli political analysts to tackle this and other questions. The Dilemmas Facing Palestinian Citizens in Israel’s Elections mloukili Thu, 10/22/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 22 October 2026 7 minutes The Dilemmas Facing Palestinian Citizens in Israel’s Elections Originally published in ISPI Arab-led parties could hold the balance of power in Israel's election. But as Palestinian citizens seek safety and equal rights, rival strategies and rejection by Jewish opposition leaders threaten to turn electoral leverage into political exclusion. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Amjad Iraqi Senior Analyst, Israel/Palestine https://x.com/aj_iraqi Related Tags Israel/Palestine In Arab towns and cities across Israel, streets and buildings are lined with posters and billboards about the upcoming national elections on 27 October. Two slates representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – a tri-party alliance called the Joint List (made up of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) and the United Arab List, also known as Ra’am – are competing for the community’s votes, which, according to polls, could give the parties a combined total of 13 to 15 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Many Palestinian citizens would agree that this election may be one of the most consequential in recent memory. But depending on who you ask, the principal contenders for their ballots appear either strikingly different or strangely similar. Despite an expanding matrix of laws and policies rendering them second-class citizens, Palestinians in Israel have long used their right to vote to assert their voice in the Knesset and to procure State resources to meet their socioeconomic needs. This year, fear has been a major driving motive . The far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has waged a relentless campaign against Palestinians – from the devastating war in Gaza, to heightened settler violence and accelerated annexation in the West Bank, to greater repression and discrimination inside Israel. Under the Ministry of National Security headed by Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s police have condoned, even more so than in the past, the organised crime and gun violence that have mushroomed in Arab localities, making personal security the top priority for most Arab voters. In theory, the Palestinian community – which makes up a fifth of Israel’s citizenry and about 17% of eligible voters – has some leverage to alter this state of affairs. Its clout derives not just from sheer numbers but from the fractured nature of Israel’s political landscape. Polls consistently show that neither Netanyahu’s ruling coalition nor the Jewish opposition led by Yashar! leader Gadi Eisenkot can secure a parliamentary majority on their own. Projections give the Joint List eight to nine seats and Ra’am five to six seats, with commentators describing the parties as potential “kingmakers” . Yet the projections tell only part of the story of a deeper schism at the heart of Palestinian politics in Israel and of the dilemmas that Arab voters face as they try to protect their rights – and indeed, their very presence – in the heart of an increasingly aggressive Israeli State. Unwanted Partners Given the likely shortfall in the Knesset, logic would dictate that the anti-Netanyahu bloc should partner with the Arab parties to oust the long-time prime minister and his far-right allies such as Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. Yet political prejudices are outweighing electoral mathematics . Almost all the Jewish opposition parties insist that they will not ally themselves with their Arab counterparts , with some even refusing to accept them as external backers of a minority government. Some, like Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, are open about their hostility towards Palestinian citizens, and some, like Together leader Naftali Bennett, worry about discouraging Jewish voters still reeling from Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks. Other still, such as Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid, are reluctant to be constrained by the demands of Arab parties. Eisenkot himself has said that he is seeking to build a “Zionist majority” coalition and that none of the Arab lists meets his criteria for partnership, such as supporting mandatory national service in the army or in civilian bodies (towards which Palestinian citizens are largely hostile), recognising Israel as a “Jewish and democratic” State (thereby accepting its ethno-nationalist character) and labelling Hamas a terrorist organisation. Split Responses Shunned and delegitimised as they are, the Joint List and Ra’am still insist they are prepared to play a part in deciding the next Israeli government. They have few illusions about an Eisenkot-led coalition, whose leaders echo many of Netanyahu’s right-wing views. Nonetheless, both Arab slates strongly believe that a renewed mandate for the far-right could amount to an existential threat to the community, let alone to Palestinians in the occupied territories. They argue that it is incumbent upon them to prevent Netanyahu’s return by any political means at their disposal. As one Arab parliamentarian put it to the International Crisis Group (ICG), “Our goal is to slow the bleeding – and I don’t mean that metaphorically”. While recognising the common danger, the two slates are at odds over how to wield their leverage . According to Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen , the tri-party alliance is ready to provide a “safety net” for an Israeli minority government as external backers in Parliament if the government pledges to tackle organised crime, halt punitive home demolitions and open a diplomatic pathway towards a Palestinian State. This offer has its antecedents: in the 1990s, Arab parties gave former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin external parliamentary support in the context of the Oslo Accords, and in 2019 and 2020, the Joint List offered its backing to Blue and White leader Benny Gantz to eject Netanyahu (which Gantz rejected). For Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas , though, any demands that relate to the occupation are likely to hinder cooperation with Jewish parties, which have grown more hawkish on the Palestinian question, at the expense of advancing the Arab community’s pressing needs. While in principle supportive of Palestinian rights and statehood, Ra’am has campaigned almost exclusively on the pledges of fighting crime and securing fresh budgets, even allying himself with former police commander and Jewish politician Yoav Segalovitz to signal that focus. Abbas, who made Ra’am a partner in the 2021-22 Bennett-Lapid government, argues that when it comes to decision making, “Either you are at the table, or you are left to the side”. Murky Prospects Experts generally agree that Palestinian citizens’ turnout at the ballot is likely to be high, with some estimating it could reach about 60-65% of eligible Arab voters. But many of those voters feel torn between two rival slates that may have little hope of acquiring the influence they claim is within their reach. If Eisenkot expects to be prime minister, he would have to either swallow his antagonism towards the Arab parties or partner with members of the rival bloc, perhaps even Netanyahu’s Likud. When faced with the same choice in 2020 after two inconclusive election rounds, Gantz opted to ally with Netanyahu. Though Eisenkot insists he will not do the same, it remains to be seen whether numerical necessity will press him toward a national unity government with Likud. Recent weeks have only deepened the murkiness. In September, with overwhelming endorsement from both coalition and opposition members, the Knesset’s Central Elections Committee disqualified the two Arab slates and two Arab politicians from running in the election. The Supreme Court overturned most of the decisions, but it supported the disqualification of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh over an article he had written describing the 7 October attacks as an “important historic event” and compelled him to either quit the race or receive a more consequential legal ruling; ultimately, he chose to bow out. Regardless of the court’s other rulings, the near-unanimous disdain towards the Arab parties delivered a chilling message that tolerance for Palestinians in the Knesset was wearing thin and that more political attacks on their representatives were likely in store. Internal disputes are also souring Arab voters. Some have been frustrated by the Joint List’s squabbles over how to allocate seats among its three parties, by a public saga over a now-ejected Hadash politician accused of sexual harassment and by disputes over the handling of Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification case. Meanwhile, some blame Ra’am for refusing to learn from the limitations it faced under the Bennett-Lapid government (such as when Ra’am members refused to join the coalition in passing a law that enshrined Israel’s ban on Palestinian family unification), for unduly taking credit for budgets secured by the Joint List in prior years, and for ignoring Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank at a time when they are being subjected to horrendous violence and suffering. Tensions Between Strategies With so much at stake, Palestinian citizens are desperate for a breakthrough in the coming elections. For some, Ra’am arguably offers the more pragmatic way forward. “The modern Arab voter is not interested in the old slogans” promoted by Arab parties, one political analyst told the International Crisis Group. Some Joint List supporters privately confess that Abbas is making a strong and coherent case for his approach. Several have even questioned the Joint List’s claim that its strategy is fundamentally different from Ra’am’s , further arguing that Ra’am’s focus on domestic issues could persuade the opposition to include it in a governing coalition and, in exchange for its support, agree to provide resources to address crime and violence – or at a minimum keep the far-right out of power. Still, Ra’am’s near-term pragmatism stands in tension with the Joint List’s long-term warning that Israel’s military rule over Palestinians beyond the Green Line cannot be detached from the shrinking rights of Palestinians inside the line. With Israel’s political spectrum sliding further rightwards, Arab parties have been among the only voices inside Israel reminding the country that the occupation is an existential problem . Ejecting the far-right could help reduce the speed and severity of Israel’s policies, but Netanyahu’s successors may prove to be almost as determined to preserve Israeli supremacy. As such, few Palestinian citizens believe that this election can bring about seismic changes. Their priorities are instead to mitigate Israel’s harms and restore some semblance of safety . The Arab parties are promising that they can advance these goals by clinching a large share of Knesset seats. Yet their voters will need other factors to make their voices count: a Jewish-Israeli politics that respects non-Jews as equals, a revitalised Palestinian leadership to guide the wider, broken national movement and a mix of international pressure and engagement to turn the conflict towards more constructive paths. REUTERS / Adnan Abidi Report 360 / Asia-Pacific 23 October 2026 20+ minutes A Trigger in Jammu and Kashmir: Militant Violence under Indian Central Rule In 2019, India made far-reaching changes to governance in Jammu and Kashmir, with the aim of quelling insurgency. Its policy has succeeded in some ways, but backfired in others. New Delhi will need to shift tack if it hopes to bring peace to the region. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags India Pakistan What’s new? Seven years after New Delhi revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status, ostensibly to curb militant activity and bring peace in its stead, disaffection is festering among Kashmiri Muslims. Militant groups are evolving in both their tactics and their chosen targets. Why does it matter? New Delhi’s tough security approach in the region has sparked a militant response. A deadly terrorist attack in April 2025 triggered clashes between India and Pakistan that ended in a stalemate. Another incident in Indian-administered Kashmir or elsewhere in India could once again trigger conflict between the two nuclear powers. What should be done? New Delhi should push forward plans to restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, hand powers back to regional authorities and rein in its harsh, counterproductive use of anti-terror laws. India and Pakistan, with the support of foreign governments, should seek to revive high-level back channels to prevent a future confrontation. Executive Summary Seven years after India revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status and ushered in sweeping reforms, ostensibly to bring peace to the Himalayan region, bitterness festers. Despite improvements in security, the changes that New Delhi foisted on the population are fuelling resentment of the Indian state while failing to uproot militant groups, which have gone underground. The repercussions go far beyond Indian-administered Kashmir. A massacre of tourists in April 2025 in the region triggered a four-day conflict between India and Pakistan after New Delhi blamed Islamabad. A ceasefire is now in place, but another terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir or elsewhere in India could unleash fresh interstate fighting. Given these risks, New Delhi should reconsider its heavy-handed approach to governance in Jammu and Kashmir. It should also restore statehood to the region, with the aim of strengthening local rule and depriving insurgents of their main rallying cry. Friendly countries should support détente between India and Pakistan, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse the potential for conflict. After proclaiming changes to Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional status in August 2019, the Indian government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), moved aggressively to pre-empt unrest, locking down public spaces, placing restrictions on communications and religious practices, and arresting politicians and activists from across the spectrum. These measures stymied opposition to New Delhi’s takeover, but they also disrupted traditional channels of political dialogue between Kashmiris and the Indian state. With protests banned and both separatist and pro-India politicians either jailed or under house arrest, channels for airing grievances were sealed shut. New Delhi ... sought to reshape Kashmiri politics by supporting new parties, sidelining established ones and redesigning constituencies to influence electoral results. New Delhi also sought to reshape Kashmiri politics by supporting new parties, sidelining established ones and redesigning constituencies to influence electoral results. Before holding regional polls in September 2024, the central government curtailed the powers of the chief minister, the highest political officeholder in the region, by shifting responsibilities to a lieutenant governor named by New Delhi. When the polls took place, Kashmiris chose to vent their fury at the central government’s policies by opposing the BJP. But with the new regional government rendered largely toothless, public discontent has not abated. Amendments to Jammu and Kashmir’s domicile and land laws, meanwhile, have aggravated locals’ feelings of impotence. The BJP government says these changes will boost economic growth, but Kashmiris are worried that New Delhi is plotting to redraw the region’s demographics by allowing non-Kashmiris to settle in India’s only Muslim-majority region. With limited political representation to count on, these concerns have been ignored by policymakers in the capital. Indian officials seem convinced they will be able to maintain control of the region through a combination of fear, force and the promise of development. But Kashmiri Muslims perceive the government’s decisions to be driven by religious discrimination, describing its approach as “collective punishment”. Though most Kashmiris abhor the killing of civilians, Crisis Group research since 2021 suggests that tacit support for militants who resort to such violence is on the rise in some quarters. While the government’s campaign has thinned their ranks, these groups are still able to carry out large-scale attacks at opportune moments. Militants, for their part, are intent on winning wider public support. New outfits with secular names such as The Resistance Front and the United Liberation Front of Kashmir have emerged, though authorities say they are merely rebranded anti-India jihadist groups operating from Pakistan, allegations that Islamabad denies. These outfits go to great lengths to conceal their activities. As India’s forces focus on the Muslim-majority Kashmir valley, militants have also increasingly turned their sights on Hindu-majority Jammu, catching authorities off guard. Tactics have changed as well. At the heart of the militants’ campaign is opposition to efforts to remake the region’s social and religious identity. A series of killings of non-local civilians by these groups, including the April 2025 massacre in Pahalgam in which 26 mostly Hindu tourists were killed, seems designed to exploit antipathy for government policies, particularly the change in legislation allowing non-Kashmiris to settle in the region. A suicide bombing that killed fifteen in November 2025 in New Delhi has likewise inflamed concerns about an uptick in jihadist violence. New Delhi’s uncompromising measures have fuelled anger in Kashmir while seemingly failing to eradicate [militant] groups. In the Indian government’s opinion, the militants’ selection of soft targets suggests that the insurgency is fading away. But New Delhi’s uncompromising measures have fuelled anger in Kashmir while seemingly failing to eradicate these groups. Accusations that Pakistan is supporting Kashmiri militants have also ratcheted up tensions with Islamabad, which rejects the allegations and attributes Kashmiri discontent to India’s heavy-handed policies in the region. Following the Pahalgam attack, New Delhi conducted airstrikes on alleged “terrorist infrastructure” in Pakistan, triggering a four-day conflict between the two nuclear-armed states that caused worldwide alarm. The display of Pakistan’s fighting capabilities during these short-lived clashes appears to have bolstered support for Islamabad among some Kashmiri Muslims, who look to Pakistan as a bulwark of resistance to New Delhi. Indeed, many locals believe Pakistan has ramped up its backing for militant groups, though they provide no conclusive evidence to that effect. New Delhi should shift tack if it wishes to bring lasting peace to the region. It should restore statehood to Jammu and Kashmir, as a first step toward reducing public distrust of the Indian state, and return powers to the chief minister in recognition of the region’s demand for greater autonomy. Indian officials should also roll back the clampdown, particularly the use of harsh anti-terror laws against anyone even suspected of militant ties. The high risk of renewed conflict between India and Pakistan also underscores the importance of resuming bilateral dialogue. Given the limited appetite in New Delhi for such engagement, quiet diplomacy through a high-level back channel remains the best option. Foreign governments with influence in both New Delhi and Islamabad should discreetly encourage the two governments to rekindle contacts that can foster mutual trust and lower the danger of a wider conflagration. After close to four decades of conflict, achieving durable peace in Indian-administered Kashmir and preventing a resumption of war with Pakistan will require bold moves that look beyond counter-insurgency and central government diktat. New Delhi/Srinagar/Brussels, 23 October 2026 Poonch district in Jammu lies on the border with Pakistan. With the security campaign focused in Kashmir, militants expanded their focus south across the Pir Panjal range to Jammu. Poonch, Jammu, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi I. Introduction For decades, Jammu and Kashmir has been a hive of separatist militancy in India and a source of friction in the country’s relations with neighbouring Pakistan. What is now Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir was once part of a princely state that was hotly disputed between India and Pakistan upon partition in 1947. For the next two years, the two countries went to war over the territory, which was split in two by a ceasefire, with both sides since claiming it in its entirety. They have clashed several times since then. In 1951, India granted semi-autonomous status to the portion of the Himalayan region it controls. This area is itself divided by topography and majority religion. Jammu, lying closer to the rest of India south of the Pir Panjal mountain range, is mostly Hindu. Muslim-majority Kashmir is nestled in a valley between the Pir Panjals and the towering Himalayas to the north and east. In 2019, the Indian government made far-reaching changes to the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir. Officials claimed that these reforms would put an end to the insurgency that had been raging against Indian rule since 1989, calling either for merging the territory with Pakistan or declaring it an independent country. In many ways, New Delhi’s intervention appears to have been successful: the frequency of militant attacks has declined, as has the number of active militants, and violent street protests have almost vanished. But in other respects, not least that popular resentment of the Indian state has intensified, the 2019 measures appear to have backfired. This report takes the political temperature in Indian-administered Kashmir seven years after New Delhi took away the region’s semi-autonomous status. It looks at the policies New Delhi has pursued in the interim and the new sorts of militancy that are emerging, despite the state’s clampdown, as a result. It then assesses the chances of further confrontations between India and Pakistan related to Kashmir, before suggesting some ways of dialling down tensions both inside and surrounding the region. The report is based on field research in both the Kashmir valley and the Jammu area, including roughly 60 interviews with state officials, Kashmiri politicians and ordinary Kashmiris. About a tenth of the interviewees were women, reflecting their low representation in the region’s public sphere.
