The report also draws upon Crisis Group’s past publications on the Kashmir dispute. 1 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°185, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , 17 September 2025; Crisis Group Statement, “ Pulling India and Pakistan Back from the Brink ”, 8 May 2025; Crisis Group Commentary, “ Keeping Kashmir on the Radar ”, 27 January 2022; Crisis Group Asia Report N°310, Raising the Stakes in Jammu and Kashmir , 5 August 2020; Crisis Group Commentary, “ Calming India and Pakistan’s Tit-for-Tat Escalation ”, 1 March 2019; Crisis Group Commentary, “ Deadly Kashmir Suicide Bombing Ratchets Up India-Pakistan Tensions ”, 22 February 2019; Crisis Group Asia Report N°224, Pakistan’s Relations with India: Beyond Kashmir? , 3 May 2012; Crisis Group Asia Report N°79, India/Pakistan Relations and Kashmir: Steps Toward Peace , 24 June 2004; Crisis Group Asia Report N°69, Kashmir: The View From New Delhi , 4 December 2003; Crisis Group Asia Report N°68, Kashmir: The View From Islamabad , 4 December 2003; Crisis Group Asia Report N°70, Kashmir: Learning from the Past , 4 December 2003; Crisis Group Asia Report N°41, Kashmir: The View From Srinagar , 21 November 2002; Crisis Group Asia Report N°35, Kashmir: Confrontation and Miscalculation , 11 July 2002. II. The Centre Takes Hold A. A Hostile Takeover On 5 August 2019, the Indian government declared that it was revoking what was commonly referred to as Article 370 – the clause in the Indian constitution that had granted semi-autonomy to the state of Jammu and Kashmir – and dividing the state into two union territories, both to be run by the central government. 2 The two union territories in question are Jammu and Kashmir, which is largely Muslim and was once a princely state, and sparsely populated Ladakh, which has a mix of Buddhists and Muslims. The central government had already dissolved the elected regional assembly in 2018, after the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) withdrew its support for the Jammu and Kashmir People’s Democratic Party, leaving it unable to muster a majority. It is likely that the BJP made this decision with an eye to minimising resistance to the forthcoming changes. For weeks prior to the announcement, the region had been on a knife’s edge. Kashmiris were rattled by several unexplained government decisions, such as asking tourists to leave the state (citing a supposed terrorist threat) and sending in an additional 40,000 troops. 3 Anuradha Bhasin, A Dismantled State: The Untold Story of Kashmir after Article 370 (Gurugram, 2023), p. 1. The valley was parcelled into small blocks, cordoned off on all sides and placed under lockdown. On 4 August, New Delhi imposed a communications blackout, cutting off the region from the rest of the world. Only the next day was it apparent that the government had taken these steps in anticipation of violent backlash to its measure revoking semi-autonomy. A local journalist described the 5 August announcement as “the biggest existential crisis” ever for Kashmiris under Indian rule, but the popular response was restrained. 4 Crisis Group interview, leading journalist, Srinagar, October 2021. Protests were certainly discouraged by the massive deployment of state forces. More important, however, was the absence of political figures who might have led the charge. As a precautionary measure, the central government had detained the entire Kashmiri political class, from pro-India mainstream politicians to separatist leaders who had boycotted electoral politics and, sometimes, embraced similar goals to the militants. 5 Most of the separatist leaders remain in jail to this day. “5161 persons taken into preventive custody in Kashmir valley since 4th August 2019: Shri. G. Kishan Reddy”, press release, Indian Ministry of Home Affairs, 4 December 2019. The harsh treatment meted out to mainstream politicians, many of whom had worked closely with central governments in the past, shocked Kashmiris, who saw it as evidence that New Delhi would never trust them, no matter how much loyalty they displayed. 6 “Ground report: Kashmir in shock and anger”, The Caravan , 16 August 2019. Three of the erstwhile state’s former chief ministers were among those detained. In hindsight, it is clear that the detentions weakened politicians who defended integration into India as the best choice for Kashmiris, as opposed to independence or joining Pakistan. 7 Prior to 2019, pro-India parties participated in elections and ran the regional government, whereas separatist forces rejected compliance with the Indian constitution. The government’s sweep did not stop at politicians, but reached into civil society as well, with figures such as journalists and human rights activists rounded up for alleged participation in separatist networks. In July 2019, before the proclamation of central rule, the National Investigation Agency, India’s top counter-terrorism and investigative body, summoned the editors of Greater Kashmir and The Kashmir Reader , two leading newspapers in the region, to question them about their sources of funding – a move that other local media outlets took as a warning. 8 Kunal Majumder, “Kashmir’s news media faces existential crisis amid restrictions, arrests”, Committee to Protect Journalists, 24 September 2019. Later, dozens of journalists were detained and investigated under severe anti-terror laws. 9 Bhasin, A Dismantled State , op. cit., pp. 161-166. The Kashmir Press Club in Srinagar was converted into a police station. By January 2020, the administration had introduced formal new restrictions on press freedom, including the threat of punishment for publishing material the authorities deemed “unethical” or “anti-national”. 10 Auqib Javed, “Kashmir’s new media policy menaces its media”, Article 14, 6 July 2020. For many Kashmiris, the fact that the clampdown was the work of a government led by the ... BJP gave it an unmistakable hue of religious discrimination. By such means, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government showed that it meant business in establishing control of India’s sole Muslim-majority region. Its approach marked a departure from previous practice, which had typically involved a combination of sleight of hand and coercion in managing conflict. For many Kashmiris, the fact that the clampdown was the work of a government led by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) gave it an unmistakable hue of religious discrimination. The closure of the Grand Mosque in Srinagar and the months-long detention of its chief cleric – Kashmir’s most prominent religious figure, known by the title Mirwaiz – deepened this impression. 11 “In Kashmir, closed mosque belies India’s religious freedom”, AP, 16 December 2021. Kashmiris were quick to dub the government’s moves “collective punishment”, saying they now lived in an “open-air prison”. 12 “Kashmir turned into an open-air prison”, Jacobin , 9 December 2019. Across the rest of India, on the other hand, public opinion proved overwhelmingly supportive of the changes imposed by New Delhi. Most Indians bought the government’s argument that its reforms were an antidote to separatism and would spur an economic boom in Kashmir. Fresh from a second successive landslide in the April-May 2019 national elections, the BJP was riding a nationalist wave. During the campaign, it had capitalised on anger about a suicide attack that had killed over 40 security personnel in Pulwama, Indian-administered Kashmir, in February 2019. 13 Crisis Group Commentary, “ Deadly Kashmir Suicide Bombing Ratchets Up India-Pakistan Tensions ”, op. cit. The BJP portrayed itself as the party that would avenge these deaths and Modi as the country’s “guardian”. 14 The BJP used the Hindi term chowkidar , which means “guard” or “watchman”. “Pakistan, terrorism, chowkidar – Modi’s favourite words in speeches after Pulwama attack”, The Print , 11 April 2019. The Pulwama attack reportedly firmed up the government’s resolve to repeal Article 370, a pledge the BJP had included in its manifesto since 1983. Rahul Pandita, The Lover Boy of Bahawalpur: How the Pulwama Case Was Cracked (New Delhi, 2021), p. 140. Much of the national media also amplified New Delhi’s contention that Kashmiris were celebrating the changes imposed upon them . 15 “ Republic World : ‘Modi corrects Nehru’s Kashmir blunder’”, video, YouTube, 6 August 2019. B. Behind the Iron Curtain Following the government’s decision to cut off internet and mobile connectivity, Kashmir became an information black hole, making it impossible to keep tabs on events as they unfolded. 16 “Kashmir group calls India’s internet ban ‘digital apartheid’”, AP, 25 August 2020. The Indian home minister was probably correct when he said Kashmir had been “integrated” without a single bullet being fired or a single person dying. 17 “Kashmir integrated without a single bullet: Amit Shah”, The Times of India , 27 October 2019. But the repression was nonetheless intense. According to the few media reports that exist, state forces went after young people from southern Kashmir, which is known for being a hotbed of separatism, beating them with sticks and rods as well as using other forms of torture, including hanging them upside down for prolonged periods and applying electric shocks, to prevent disturbances. 18 See, for example, “With meticulous planning, then mass arrests, and ‘torture’, Kashmir’s autonomy was lost”, The Independent , 1 September 2019; “The night the soldiers came: Allegations of abuse surface in Kashmir”, The Washington Post , 30 September 2019; “‘Don’t beat us, just shoot us’: Kashmiris allege violent crackdown”, BBC, 30 August 2019. Fact-finding reports by civil society organisations also noted cases of sexual harassment of Kashmiri women during search operations conducted at night. 19 Crisis Group interview, woman student from Pulwama district, Srinagar, November 2025. Due to social stigma among the Muslims of Kashmir, violence against women often goes unreported. See Bhasin, A Dismantled State , op. cit., pp. 76-77; and “Annual Human Rights Review 2019”, Jammu and Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society, December 2019. Seven years later, many such incidents have not yet come to light. A senior journalist quoted the Kashmiri poet Agha Shahid Ali (himself echoing Tacitus) when reflecting on New Delhi’s assertion of control: “They make a desolation and call it peace”. 20 Crisis Group interview, leading journalist, Srinagar, August 2023. Soon after imposing a national lockdown in March 2020 following the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Indian government pushed through further changes. A week into the lockdown, New Delhi amended Jammu and Kashmir’s domicile law, making Indians from other parts of the country eligible for permanent residency in the territory, as well as for public-sector jobs. 21 The government enabled itself repealing Article 35A of the constitution – which defined who was a permanent resident of Jammu and Kashmir and their rights, and restricted non-residents from holding government jobs or owning land within the state – along with Article 370. The move unnerved Kashmiris, who perceived it as the first step in a campaign to alter the region’s demographics to the detriment of local Muslims. 22 Crisis Group interviews, locals including journalists, officials and political leaders, Kashmir, 2019-2025. In October, New Delhi announced new laws allowing non-residents to purchase land in the region, even though Jammu and Kashmir, along with a few other states, had long enjoyed special protections to safeguard its culture. 23 “Ominously anti-federal: On the Supreme Court’s judgment on Article 370 and J&K’s special status”, The Hindu , 12 December 2023; “What is Article 371 and what are the protections it provides?”, The Hindu , 9 May 2024. With no elected representatives to appeal to or channels for conveying their discontent, Kashmiris grew increasingly convinced that the government was intent on bringing in non-Kashmiris to convert them into a minority. 24 “India’s residency law in Kashmir amplifies demographic fears”, AP, 5 August 2020. Under house arrest, Kashmir’s pre-eminent separatist leader, Syed Ali Geelani, who had long warned of such a risk, urged people to resist the reforms. 25 “Hurriyat leader Syed Ali Shah Geelani asks Kashmiris to resist, issues ‘program of action’”, Scroll.in , 25 August 2019. “J&K: Geelani sees plot to change Muslim majority”, The New Indian Express , 16 May 2012. The government then started to redraw electoral constituencies in Jammu and Kashmir. It justified the move as part of the reorganisation initiated in 2019, but locals perceived it as gerrymandering intended to benefit the BJP – which, as a Hindu nationalist party, is more influential in the Hindu-majority Jammu region than in the Muslim-majority Kashmir valley – and yet another measure designed to deprive them of a political voice. 26 Praveen Donthi, “ Flare-Ups and Frustration as Kashmir Waits for a Vote ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 8 March 2024. The delimitation commission appointed by the government eventually added six new constituencies to the Jammu division and only one to the Kashmir division, which has a larger population but is 97 per cent Muslim, leading to accusations that the commission was acting in the BJP’s service. 27 Ibid. The population of Jammu stands at 5.3 million, whereas that of the Kashmir valley is 6.8 million. Those charged with delimitation should normally redraw electoral constituencies according to population size, to ensure that each elected representatives correspond has roughly an equal number of constituents. In combination, the closure of avenues of political representation, the crackdown on dissent and the battery of other reforms heightened Kashmiris’ anxiety about the future. For some of them, these developments also gave rise to a newfound sympathy for militant groups. 28 In the only Srinagar neighbourhood to witness protests in August 2019, demonstrators chanted the slogan, “One solution, gun solution”. See “Ground report: Kashmir in shock and anger”, op. cit. It may have been a sign of things to come. C. Seeking International Attention Kashmiris hoped that Pakistan – and its close ally China – would intervene in international forums to draw attention to the region’s plight. Both countries did indeed raise concerns about India’s actions at the UN. Asserting that any change in Jammu and Kashmir’s disputed status violated UN resolutions, Islamabad downgraded its diplomatic relations with New Delhi and expelled the Indian high commissioner; India responded in kind. Imran Khan, Pakistan’s prime minister, penned an op-ed in The New York Times , warning that if the world did not “stop the Indian assault on Kashmir” it would face “consequences … as two nuclear-armed states get ever closer to a direct military confrontation”. 29 Imran Khan, “The world can’t ignore Kashmir: We are all in danger”, The New York Times , 30 August 2019. Beijing also sharply criticised New Delhi, telling the UN Security Council that India had “challenged China’s sovereign interests” and was stoking regional tensions. 30 China holds an area called Aksai Chin, which was part of Jammu and Kashmir when it was a princely state. Beijing seized these lands in the 1962 Sino-Indian war; New Delhi claims them as part of Ladakh. “UNSC Kashmir moot gives lie to Indian claim”, Dawn , 17 August 2019; “Chinese Stance in United Nations Security Council towards India”, Vivekananda International Foundation, 15 October 2020. Despite these condemnations, many Kashmiris were disappointed that Islamabad failed to mobilise meaningful international pressure on India to reverse its actions. 31 Crisis Group interviews, Kashmiri residents, Srinagar, November 2023. Their sense of abandonment only deepened when Prime Minister Modi, visiting Washington in September 2019, announced that India was building a “new Kashmir”, getting no pushback from U.S. officials. 32 Crisis Group interviews, journalists, academics and politicians, Srinagar, 2021. “We will build a ‘new’ Kashmir for everyone says PM Modi to Kashmiri pandits in Houston”, The Hindu , 22 September 2019. New Delhi’s post-2019 security crackdown in Jammu and Kashmir suppressed militancy, but militants remain capable of conducting big attacks like in Pahalgam of April 2025. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi III. Politics and Militants in the “New Kashmir” As India’s central government tightened its grip on Kashmir, fear grew among locals that New Delhi was intent on transforming the Muslim-majority region. With little support for its cause among Kashmiris, New Delhi opted to continue ruling the region through its appointed representative. Meanwhile, its stranglehold on Kashmir forced militants to change their tactics, posing new challenges to Indian authorities. A. Re-engineering the Political Landscape After altering the status of Jammu and Kashmir, the federal government sought to bring about a new political configuration in the region, one that New Delhi would find “absolutely pliable”, as a Kashmiri journalist put it. 33 Crisis Group interview, leading Kashmiri journalist, Srinagar, 2023. While prominent local leaders remained under arrest and political activity was curtailed, new parties favoured by the central government endeavoured to win public support. They failed to do so, however, as the vast majority of Kashmiris perceived them as BJP proxies. 34 Bhasin, A Dismantled State , op. cit., p. 188. Alongside its support for new parties, the Indian government sought to redraw electoral constituencies for regional and national elections (see Section II.B). 35 “Jammu and Kashmir: The hidden agenda behind the delimitation exercise”, Frontline , 2 April 2022. The BJP hoped that the extra seats it created in Jammu would help it secure a majority in the regional assembly once new elections were called, enabling it to establish an administration that would not depend on coalitions with Kashmiri parties. New Delhi nevertheless appeared uncertain that the new formula would deliver. It remained reluctant to hold regional elections until the Supreme Court ordered it to do so by September 2024. 36 Ibid. The first major polls held in Jammu and Kashmir after the 2019 changes were the national parliamentary elections, which took place in June 2024. Aware of popular anger at the central government, the BJP did not contest the region’s three national constituencies. One of the region’s two largest parties and its oldest, the Jammu and Kashmir National Conference, won two, while Kashmiris sent an emphatic message to Indian authorities in the third by electing an independent, Sheikh Abdul Rashid, a 58-year-old politician who had been in jail since August 2019 on charges of “terror funding” and receiving funds from Pakistan. 37 Rashid remains in prison, but the court allows him to attend parliamentary proceedings in police custody. “‘Vote against jail’: How two Modi critics won India election from prison”, Al Jazeera, 14 June 2024; “Kashmir: Why Modi’s BJP is not fighting elections in the Himalayan region”, BBC, 11 May 2024. Defiant, he called his win “a referendum against all sorts of oppression” and said the calm in Kashmir should not be interpreted as “real peace”. 38 “Engineer Rashid delivers victory message with a sting”, The Telegraph , 12 June 2024. Voter discontent was ... plain to see in the regional polls in September, which saw a high turnout of 63 per cent. Voter discontent was also plain to see in the regional polls in September, which saw a high turnout of 63 per cent. Though they had previously called on Kashmiris to boycott elections, separatist politicians backed the vote on this occasion, arguing that citizens needed an administration run by locals, which could provide a measure of relief from constant repression, rather than bureaucrats who had parachuted in. 39 Praveen Donthi, “ Kashmir Votes to Repudiate Rule from the Centre ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 October 2024. Voter participation in elections held in Jammu and Kashmir has historically been scant – as low as 3 per cent in one constituency in 2002 – due to factors ranging from separatism to fear of militant attack. Turnout was exceptionally high in the two most recent votes: 58 per cent for the national elections in April-May 2024 and 63 per cent during that October’s regional elections. “Jammu and Kashmir polls: Ups and downs in voter turnout”, The Hindu , 8 October 2024. The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference won 42 of 90 seats, becoming the largest political force in the new regional assembly; the party’s leader, Omar Abdullah, was elected chief minister – a position he had already held more than a decade ago. The BJP finished second with 29 seats, all of them in Hindu-majority Jammu, not Kashmir. “People responded to an undemocratic decision through democratic means, by registering their dissent”, a Kashmiri member of the federal parliament observed. 40 Crisis Group interview, Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, member of parliament, Budgam, 28 November 2025. Even so, the authority of the new regional assembly and the chief minister had been curbed well before the polls were held. The 2019 reforms had already diluted regional powers by turning the state into a union territory. Security and law enforcement, particularly land laws, fell under the purview of a lieutenant governor appointed by New Delhi. Between 2019 and the 2024 elections, New Delhi extended the lieutenant governor’s remit to include a final say on most legislative and administrative matters. By allowing normal political activity to resume, the vote opened space for public debate. But Kashmiris remain deeply dissatisfied with a setup they see as entrenching rule by outsiders. 41 Crisis Group interviews, journalists, politicians and academics, Srinagar, 2021-2025. Furthermore, the elected chief minister has few prerogatives, particularly as regards security. “Having two power centres anywhere is a recipe for disaster”, Chief Minister Abdullah himself commented. 42 “‘Recipe for disaster’: CM Omar Abdullah on dual governance model in J&K”, The Times of India , 14 December 2024. Having served in the post once before, he is well placed to understand the difference: when Jammu and Kashmir was a state, his office served as head of the unified command, integrating all the state’s security forces. Now, not only does he have no say in security matters, but he also lacks input into minor decisions such as appointing civil servants. 43 “‘Families devastated, review each case’: From Mehbooba to Omar, a letter on termination of 74 employees without hearing”, The Indian Express , 11 November 2024; “Raj Bhawan’s actions undermine elected government in J&K: Omar Abdullah”, The Hindu , 29 November 2025. B. A Chokehold on Militancy New Delhi’s post-2019 crackdown in Jammu and Kashmir suppressed militancy, but it did not put an end to this activity. State forces invoked two stringent anti-terror laws – the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act – which allow for holding detainees for up to six months without formal charges or trial. 44 “The UAPA and PSA are being used as tools of coercion in Kashmir”, Frontline , 23 March 2021. Beyond dismantling what it called the “terror ecosystem”, the government’s objective was also to “increase the social costs for supporting or becoming a militant”. 45 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Srinagar, 2025. The state started prosecuting anyone remotely linked to militants or their alleged associates, rather than just their immediate family and friends, as had long been the case. 46 Ibid. According to official data, 3,662 people have been arrested under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act between 2019 and 2023. No official data is available regarding arrests made under the Public Safety Act; however, according to media reports, at least 4,000 people were detained under this law in August 2019, and most recently the chief minister claimed that 400 people were in prison under it. See “J&K accounts for 35% of all UAPA arrests in India from 2019-2023, data reveals”, The New Indian Express , 4 December 2025; “At least 4,000 detained in Kashmir since region stripped of autonomy”, AFP, 18 August 2019; and “J&K CM Omar flags misuse of Public Safety Act against youth with no cases, claims 400 such arrests”, The Hindu , 7 March 2025. Firmly under New Delhi’s control, the regional authorities even dismissed public employees for security reasons, without due process. 47 See tweet by Omar Abdullah, @OmarAbdullah, former chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir, 8:22pm, 8 June 2024. The government took several other measures to quash militancy. For instance, state forces stopped returning slain militants’ bodies to their families, citing pandemic rules. The real reason, however, was that funerals had become occasions to lionise militants and inspire disgruntled young people to join the fight. 48 Not handing over dead bodies offended the religious sensibilities of Kashmiri people. “Kashmir: Why is anger rising over militant burials?”, Deutsche Welle, 30 November 2021. Soldiers also systematically demolished the houses of suspected militants’ families, as well as those of individuals suspected of aiding the insurgency in any way. 49 Bhasin, A Dismantled State , p. 121. These punitive measures served to stoke antipathy toward the Indian state. 50 “Youth share tales of harassment at PDP meet on why Kashmiri professionals are turning to violence”, The Hindu , 8 December 2025. In response, insurgents modified their tactics. Soon after August 2019, novel outfits with secular names such as The Resistance Front, the Kashmir Tigers, the People’s Anti-Fascist Front and the United Liberation Front of Kashmir emerged, emphasising opposition to the government’s efforts to alter the region’s socio-religious identity rather than the traditional separatist themes. 51 Crisis Group Report, Raising the Stakes in Jammu and Kashmir, op. cit. The message was designed to resonate with Kashmiris fearful that New Delhi was engineering demographic change. Many Kashmiris condemned [the militants' killings of "outsiders"], while continuing to oppose New Delhi’s legislative changes. A series of attacks mirrored the switch in rhetoric. From October 2019, militants killed a number of non-locals in the south of Indian-administered Kashmir, gunning down fruit traders and truck drivers, as well as migrant labourers – most of them Hindus, though the victims also included non-Kashmiri Muslims. 52 The number of militant attacks on state forces continued but declined slightly after 2019. Attacks on non-local civilians and local police officers increased, however. For instance, between 2014 and 2019, militants killed 170 civilians and 406 security personnel, but between August 2019 and November 2021 they killed 87 civilians and 99 security personnel. The gap between the number of civilian and security personnel deaths narrowed most in 2021 and 2022: 41 civilians and 42 security personnel were killed in 2021, and 31 and 32, respectively, in 2022. This trend continued from 2023 to 2025, when 73 civilians and 72 security personnel were killed. See “87 civilians, 99 security personnel killed in J&K since Article 370 scrapped: Govt”, The Hindu , 6 April 2022; “Security situation in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh”, press release, Indian Ministry of Home Affairs, 7 February 2024. Militants also began to deliberately attack the few Kashmiri Hindus who had not fled during the mass exodus in 1990 or had come back later. 53 The vast majority of Kashmiri pandits, as members of Jammu and Kashmir’s Hindu community are known, fled the region in the early 1990s due to militant threats. See Praveen Donthi, “ Violence in Kashmir: Why a Spike in Killings Signals Ominous New Trend ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 28 June 2022. While not all these victims would have been eligible for residency or jobs under Jammu and Kashmir’s new domicile laws introduced in 2020, the systematic targeting of “outsiders” sent an intimidating message to non-locals. Many Kashmiris condemned these killings, while continuing to oppose New Delhi’s legislative changes. Another trend that briefly emerged after 2019 was a series of assaults on Kashmiri police officers. 54 Crisis Group interview, mid-level security official, Srinagar, 2023. See also Donthi, “ Flare-Ups and Frustration as Kashmir Waits for a Vote ”, op. cit. Separatist leaders, who wielded influence over militants, had previously discouraged attacks on police on the grounds that, unlike Indian army soldiers, they are mostly locals; they feared that such incidents could spark intra-communal conflict. But with all the separatist leaders jailed in the aftermath of New Delhi’s intervention, the safeguard disappeared. A police officer told Crisis Group that the force used to be able to press separatist leaders into convincing militants not to attack its personnel. But the sudden changes in circumstances have meant the police are “playing a game without a referee”, demoralising the rank and file. 55 Ibid. New Delhi painted the militants’ choice of soft targets such as non-locals and police officers as a sign of weakness, asserting that a lack of weaponry, training and numbers had dissuaded them from attacking Indian security forces. Though this claim may have an element of truth, the full picture is more complex. One security official told Crisis Group that the militants’ aim in harming civilians was to trigger a disproportionate state response, in the belief that mass arrests would foster further disaffection with Indian authorities and support for insurgent groups. 56 Crisis Group interview, security official, Srinagar, 2023. Others believe the attacks may have been a cheap and easy means of discrediting the government’s narrative about achieving peace in Kashmir, as they made national and international headlines. 57 Crisis Group interviews, senior security officials, Jammu and Kashmir, 2023. The militants killed five non-local labourers on the day a delegation of EU parliamentarians visited Kashmir in October 2019, likely as a way of drawing international attention. See “Outrage over right-wing Euro MPs’ Kashmir visit”, BBC, 31 October 2019. The central government said its iron-fist approach of “comprehensively defeating” separatism was working, however, in part because it had countered the “substantial influence of Pakistan” on both Kashmiri public opinion and militant groups. 58 “The Straight Line: Pak control, narrative war, white-collar terror: Ex DGP of J&K R. S. Swain’s first big interview”, video, YouTube, 20 January 2026. Given the long history in Kashmir of protests spiralling out of control, the official priority was to “ensure the streets remain calm”. 59 Ibid. With the stone throwing, Kashmiri youth were modelling themselves on Palestinians during the two intifadas. In that regard, the crackdown was indeed successful: it is now rare for demonstrators to pelt state forces with stones, as they did regularly in the past. 60 Crisis Group interview, mid-level security official, Srinagar, 2025. But the change did not put an end to militancy in Kashmir, which appears to have adapted to the new environment. C. A New Breed of Insurgents? Over the decade leading up to 2019, militants were largely locals who openly used social media and relied on overground networks for logistics and recruitment. After New Delhi stepped up its counter-insurgency campaign in August 2019, militants not only altered their tactics, but they also went deep underground, becoming “lone wolves” who leave few physical or digital traces, making it much harder to pursue them. 61 Of late, militants have also avoided using intermediaries who can be monitored or technology that can be tracked. Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Jammu and Kashmir, Srinagar, November 2023-November 2025. Indian officials say many of the attacks that followed imposition of central rule were perpetrated by young people with no prior links to militancy – a profile they describe as the “hybrid militant”. 62 Some Indian officials claim that Pakistan-based militant groups are behind this tactical shift. “Hybrid militancy a ‘strategic move’ by Pakistan: J&K police chief”, Deccan Herald , 22 July 2022; “Shadow militants: Why a policeman’s killing has shaken a battle-hardened Kashmiri village”, Scroll.in , 16 August 2022. Officials allege that these recruits have often carried out a single attack, at the behest of Pakistani handlers, and then returned to their normal lives. 63 “Inside the shadowy, deadly world of Kashmir’s teenage hybrid militants”, Article 14 , 6 October 2022. A second change in militancy after August 2019 relates to its geographic spread. As New Delhi focused its campaign on the Kashmir valley, militants increasingly staged their attacks in the Jammu region, south of the valley across the Pir Panjal mountains. The first major ambush in Jammu took place in October 2021, when militants killed five soldiers, gunning down four more during the search operation that followed. 64 “New terror push in Jammu, Gujjar, Bakherwal alienation: Why the deaths of 5 soldiers underline the security challenge in Poonch”, The Indian Express , 5 May 2023. The militants’ rationale for extending their fight southward was likely twofold: a recalibration to escape the larger troop deployment and a wish to spare Kashmiri Muslims the state’s reprisals. 65 Crisis Group interviews, security officials and civil society figures, Jammu and Srinagar, December 2025. The magnitude of the challenge became clear as the encounters with state forces increased. Attacks in Jammu, which had been formally declared free of militancy in 2020, accounted for 40 per cent of all security personnel killed in Jammu and Kashmir between 2021 and 2024. 66 “Since 2021, Jammu accounts for 40% of killings of security personnel in J&K”, The Hindu , 17 July 2024. By 2025, a senior police officer said, the authorities were conducting an average of 120 anti-militancy operations per day in the region. 67 “120 anti-terror ops launched daily in Jammu to eliminate foreign terrorists: IGP”, Greater Kashmir , 21 October 2025. The resurgence of violence in Jammu after almost two decades of peace caught the Indian security establishment off guard. The resurgence of violence in Jammu after almost two decades of peace caught the Indian security establishment off guard. State forces had grown complacent amid the peace that had prevailed in the decade prior to 2019. Their numbers had also been depleted in 2020, when New Delhi transferred troops to Ladakh after the border clash with Chinese troops that April. 68 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Report N°334, Thin Ice in the Himalayas: Handling the India-China Border Dispute , 14 November 2023. Crucial intelligence networks also broke down following the declaration of central rule over the region. Time and again, the authorities found that their old informers were acting as double agents for the militants. By 2020, the Jammu and Kashmir security apparatus decided to stop relying on informers, notwithstanding the ill effects on their intelligence-gathering capabilities. 69 Many smugglers who had been acting as informers were also cast aside. Crisis Group interview, security official, Jammu, 2025. Later, New Delhi also lost the services of the Gujjars and Bakkarwals, two nomadic tribes who live at high altitudes and had long been the state’s eyes and ears along remote border stretches, particularly as regards early warning of infiltration from Pakistan. These tribes were disgruntled by Indian government actions in the region. When they proved disinclined to cooperate with the authorities, officers suspected them of aiding the militants and meted out punishments allegedly including extrajudicial killings, exacerbating their estrangement from the state. 70 Gujjars and Bakkarwals make up 12 per cent of the population in Jammu and Kashmir. Their discontent stems from the BJP’s decision to grant Scheduled Tribe status, which confers benefits such as quotas for government jobs, to another ethnic group in 2023, sowing fear among them that their own share of these benefits would be reduced. “A people without voice: Why are Gujjars in Jammu region feeling under siege?”, Scroll.in , 8 October 2017; “Gujjar-Bakarwal agitation: Why Kashmiri tribals are up in arms”, Frontline , 10 August 2023. On the crackdown, see “From Where the Orders Came: Army officers testify that two generals oversaw the torture and murder of civilians in Poonch”, The Caravan , 1 February 2025; “‘Extra-judicial’ killings can alienate Gujjars from security forces: Intel”, The Tribune , 28 July 2025. By 2023, militant attacks had become so regular in Jammu that the government was forced to revive a defunct militia known as the Village Defence Guards, arming and training hundreds of villagers across the region. 71 These militias were first formed in the mid-1990s, at the height of the Kashmiri insurgency, but the government disbanded them when militancy declined. “India revives civil militia after Hindu killings in Kashmir”, AP, 28 February 2023. On 9 June 2024, just hours after Prime Minister Modi was sworn in for a third consecutive term, militants assailed a bus carrying Hindu pilgrims, killing nine and injuring more than 30 in Jammu’s Reasi district. 72 “Terrorist attack at Reasi sets alarm bells ringing in India’s security establishment”, The Diplomat , 20 June 2024. The attack appeared to have been timed to contradict the government’s narrative of a peaceful region open for visitors. 73 Crisis Group noted in 2022 that tourists “could well become targets, particularly if the government continues to insist that robust tourism is a sign of normalcy”. See Praveen Donthi, “ Violence in Kashmir: Why a Spike in Killings Signals Ominous New Trend ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 28 June 2022. Before becoming chief minister, Omar Abdullah also cautioned that by “[linking] tourism with normalcy, [officials] put tourists in danger”. See “Tourist arrivals in Kashmir not an accurate gauge of normalcy: Omar Abdullah”, Business Standard , 20 May 2024. Indian officials, for their part, have blamed the spike in violence in Jammu on Pakistan-based militants sneaking across the border. 74 “Jammu and Kashmir: Surge in attacks brings fear to calmer parts of Himalayan territory”, BBC, 23 July 2024. D. “Foreign Militants” Indian officials say the outfits attacking non-locals in Indian-administered Kashmir (and increasingly in Jammu) are not new, but the same groups that Pakistan has long supported, above all Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, just with new names. According to New Delhi, both groups rebranded themselves to enable Islamabad to evade scrutiny by the Financial Action Task Force over allegations of funding terrorist groups. 75 The Task Force had until October 2022 placed Pakistan on its grey list for failing to curb money laundering and financing of these outfits. “Pakistan is out of FATF ‘grey list’ on terror funding”, The Hindu , 22 October 2022. Furthermore, Indian officials allege, “foreign militants” have assumed increasing responsibilities in these organisations of late. They claim that the militants allegedly infiltrating Jammu are more dangerous than their predecessors, mainly because they seem well trained and the police cannot track them through family connections. “Some of the old tactics are back”, a retired police chief of Jammu and Kashmir observed, referring to the period from the 1990s to the early 2000s, when Jammu was rife with militancy, and Pakistanis made up a sizeable portion of militant ranks “So we also need to revisit the old tactics and learnings on our side”. 76 “Pak control, narrative war, white-collar terror: Ex-DGP of J&K R. S. Swain’s first big interview”, op. cit. Indian officials also claim that these “foreign militants” have sophisticated weapons, and are adept at avoiding detection, particularly by using encrypted Chinese satellite phones (part of the BeiDou network) whose transmissions are difficult to intercept. 77 Militants have been found using weapons such as U.S.-made M4 assault rifles. Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Jammu and Srinagar, 2025. See also “US arms left in Afghanistan are turning up in a different conflict”, NBC News, 30 January 2023; and “Hard-to-crack Chinese devices part of terror toolkit,” The Economic Times , 30 April 2025. If true, it would be a striking evolution from the years before 2019, when militants were largely untrained and poorly equipped locals. By the end of 2023, Indian forces say, “foreign militants” had come to outnumber local insurgents. 78 “Security situation improved significantly in J&K in 2023; foreign terrorists our target for 2024, says DGP”, The Hindu , 31 December 2023. After the deadly terror attack in Pahalgam in 2025, New Delhi was quick to hold Pakistan responsible, though it has yet to present any concrete evidence to back its accusations. 79 “A year on, India has failed to substantiate allegations against Pakistan over Pahalgam attack: info minister”, Dawn , 22 May 2026. The government’s determination to pacify Kashmir led to broad anti-terror laws, which locals view as collective punishment, fuelling resentment against the Indian state and proving counterproductive. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi IV. The India-Pakistan Fault Line Kashmir’s conflict is inseparable from the dispute between India and Pakistan, which have already waged two wars (1947-1948 and 1965) over the territory and made several smaller forays into armed conflict. A third war erupted in 1971, after India intervened militarily on behalf of the Bengali struggle for independence in Pakistan’s eastern wing, which led soon thereafter to sovereignty for Bangladesh. 80 From May to July 1999, the sides clashed in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kargil district, with hundreds of soldiers killed. In 2019, they engaged in short-lived air combat following an attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 40 Indian troops. In April 2025, the militant attack on Indian tourists in Pahalgam in southern Kashmir triggered the most serious fighting between the two neighbours in decades, after India blamed Pakistan for the massacre. Four days of hostilities ended with a ceasefire on 10 May. Though New Delhi promised systematic retaliation against Islamabad if further attacks occurred on its soil, it stayed its hand when young Kashmiris carried out a suicide bombing in New Delhi on 10 November 2025. With India continuing to claim that Pakistan uses anti-India jihadist groups to wage a proxy war in Kashmir, another terror attack in the region or elsewhere in India could threaten a fragile ceasefire. A. The Pahalgam Attack and Its Aftermath The 22 April 2025 attack in Pahalgam, which saw militants shoot 26 people at point-blank range at a popular tourist destination in southern Kashmir, was the deadliest attack on civilians in over two decades. Most of the victims were Hindu tourists, whose religion the militants ascertained before gunning them down. 81 The victims also included a local Kashmiri who tried to intervene and an Indian Christian. Praveen Donthi, “Deadly Kashmir Militant Attack Raises Temperature Between India and Pakistan”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 April 2025. The Indian government immediately blamed Pakistan, alleging that it wanted to “undermine normalcy returning to Jammu and Kashmir”, disrupt the economy and “create a fertile ground for continued cross-border terrorism”. 82 “Transcript of Special Briefing on OPERATION SINDOOR”, Indian Ministry of External Affairs, 7 May 2025. Hours after the attack, New Delhi further downgraded diplomatic ties with Islamabad, shut Indian airspace to Pakistan-registered aircraft, closed the only border crossing and suspended the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty. Islamabad responded in kind. Denying Indian allegations that the Pahalgam assailants had any cross-border connections, Islamabad accused New Delhi of making these charges without evidence, while rejecting Pakistan’s suggestions of an independent international investigation into the attack. 83 On 26 April, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Islamabad was open to participating in any neutral, transparent and credible investigation of the attack. “PM Shehbaz says Pakistan open to credible, transparent probe into Pahalgam attack”, Dawn , 26 April 2025. New Delhi regarded Islamabad’s offer as disingenuous, pointing to its record of supporting anti-Indian jihadist proxies. Islamabad insisted in turn that the Modi government’s belligerent rhetoric was intended to whip up nationalist sentiment as it planned a military attack on Pakistan. 84 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, Indian forces detained thousands of Kashmiris, informing the media that the attackers had been locals. 85 “If the photographs didn’t belong to the Pahalgam attackers, what were the actions based on?”, Kashmir Times , 4 July 2025. State forces destroyed the houses of at least six suspected local militants. But the National Investigation Agency eventually listed seven accused, including the Pakistan-based heads of Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and The Resistance Front; it concluded that three Pakistanis had carried out the attack, while two local Kashmiris had provided them with food and shelter. 86 “NIA charges four LeT-TRF terrorists in Pahalgam attack”, The Hindu , 16 December 2025. In July 2025, India claimed to have killed all three of the Pakistanis, though without making the evidence public, and arrested the two Kashmiris allegedly involved. 87 Addressing parliament, Home Minister Amit Shah said security forces had established that the assailants were Pakistanis because they found Pakistani voter cards and chocolates made in Pakistan on the bodies. No further evidence was provided. “Three Pakistani terrorists behind Pahalgam terror attack killed in Operation Mahadev, centre tells Lok Sabha”, The Hindu , 29 July 2025. The terror attack on tourists visiting from throughout India, most of whom were shot dead in front of their families, shocked Kashmiris, who organised spontaneous protests condemning the killings. Many locals were also apprehensive about the backlash they knew was coming. Notwithstanding widespread public condemnation of the massacre, a section of Kashmiri society, according to a leading journalist in the region, viewed it as a consequence of New Delhi’s stranglehold on the region. 88 Crisis Group interview, senior Kashmiri journalist, 2025. Throughout the rest of India, the killings provoked a furore, as well as mounting pressure on the government to retaliate against Pakistan. On 7 May, India launched Operation Sindoor, carrying out cross-border strikes on what it claimed was “terrorist infrastructure” across the border. This first salvo gave rise to a short but fierce exchange of fire, in which the two sides carried out tit-for-tat attacks using weaponised drones and missiles deep inside each other’s territory and across the Line of Control, the informal frontier that separates the Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts of Jammu and Kashmir. 89 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. The ceasefire froze the conflict, with both sides claiming victory, but it did not stop either from continuing its hostile posturing. After four days of conflict, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the two countries had agreed to a ceasefire, which Indian and Pakistani authorities confirmed. New Delhi said it was the Pakistani military that had requested the truce through a hotline between the directors general of military operations – the only official line of communication between the two countries. Pakistan claimed that India had reached out to it first. The ceasefire froze the conflict, with both sides claiming victory, but it did not stop either from continuing its hostile posturing. 90 Ibid. Prime Minister Modi declared that India would from now on systematically strike back against not just those perpetrating terrorist attacks on Indian soil, but also their backers – a clear allusion to Pakistan. 91 Ibid. These clashes were traumatic for many Indians, particularly in regions which endured missile and drone strikes for the first time. Many Kashmiris experienced it differently, however. Seeing Pakistani drones in their skies, hovering above and firing upon Indian installations in the region, seems to have made an impression on local people. The display of Pakistan’s military capabilities on the first day of the conflict, when it allegedly shot down several Indian fighter jets, likewise had a notable effect on local public opinion. 92 See “Pak’s Fatah 1 rocket debris fished out of Srinagar’s Dal Lake during clean-up”, India Today , 22 September 2025. “The May conflict countered post-2019 hopelessness that Pakistan is not interested in Kashmir”, a Srinagar resident observed. 93 Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. B. Weighing the Pakistani Role India insists that Pakistan is responsible for almost all militant attacks in the region, accusing Islamabad of fighting a proxy war in Kashmir, using anti-India jihadist groups such as the Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad. Indian officials also claim that Pakistani fighters are steadily infiltrating Jammu and Kashmir. 94 An Indian security official claimed that there were about 100 foreign (meaning Pakistani) militants in Kashmir. Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. Concurring with these allegations, a section of Kashmiris also say Pakistan-based jihadist groups, working at Islamabad’s behest, are now spearheading the insurgency in Kashmir. 95 Crisis Group interviews, Srinagar, 2025. Until recently, Kashmiris had disputed Indian government claims, regarding them as simplistic, albeit without denying Pakistani influence. Instead, they pointed to local young people joining militant ranks out of anger at Indian policies toward the region (see Section III.C). Nowadays, however, many claim that Pakistan is back in the driver’s seat. Establishing the truth regarding these allegations is no easy matter. Pakistan categorically denies India’s claims that it is waging a proxy war in Indian-administered Kashmir. 96 “Pakistan takes ‘strong exception’ to ‘baseless claims’ of Indian army chief”, The News , 15 January 2025. It has repeatedly said it opposes any form of terrorism, and it argues it has clamped down on homegrown jihadist groups blamed for terrorist attacks in India. 97 “Nuclear war ‘wasn’t an option’”, Dawn , 14 May 2025; “FO says Pakistan has ‘dismantled’ terrorist outfits amid U.S. designation of group blamed for Pahalgam attack”, Dawn , 18 July 2025. Lashkar-e-Tayyaba was officially banned in 2002, following an attack on the Indian parliament, as was Jaish-e-Mohammad in 2008 after another in Mumbai. When the groups attempted a comeback under new names, these were also outlawed; Lashkar-e-Tayyaba’s charity front, Jamaat-ud-Dawa, was proscribed in 2008 and Jaish-e-Mohammad’s so-called philanthropic arm, the Falah-i-Insaniyat Foundation, in 2019. The next year, the government froze the properties and assets of both groups. Islamabad also says the leaders and activists of these groups are under house arrest or jailed, including Lashkar-e-Tayyaba chief Hafiz Saeed, whom India now holds responsible for the Pahalgam attack. Convicted of terrorism financing in 2019, Saeed is in prison serving a 33-year sentence. 98 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. The fact that banned anti-India jihadist groups have proven capable of repeatedly re-emerging, only to be outlawed again, tends to undermine Pakistan’s claims that it has eliminated their organisational structures altogether. That said, it does not constitute definitive proof of New Delhi’s allegations that Islamabad is once again waging a proxy war in Jammu and Kashmir, including by sending in jihadist proxies. Pakistani experts say such a policy would undermine the country’s national security and damage its international standing. 99 Crisis Group telephone interviews, Pakistani analysts, August 2026. Islamabad claims that India is backing proxies fighting Pakistan in [Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces]. Top Pakistani policymakers reportedly feel that any armed venture could spark conflict with India, leaving the country open to a two-front threat at a time when it confronts a raging insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces, bordering Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, where militant attacks have killed thousands of Pakistan’s security personnel and civilians. 100 Crisis Group telephone interview, August 2026. See also Crisis Group Asia Report N°354, Pakistan: Responding to the Militant Surge on the Afghan Border , 27 February 2026. Islamabad claims that India is backing proxies fighting Pakistan in these regions via its close ties with the Afghan Talban authorities and support for anti-Pakistani insurgents on Afghan soil, namely Baloch militant groups and the jihadist Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (or Pakistani Taliban). 101 Islamabad, however, holds Kabul primarily responsible, alleging that the Afghan Taliban provide safe havens to Pakistani militant groups. “Naqvi holds India responsible for spate of attacks in Balochistan: ISPR says 92 terrorists killed”, Dawn , 31 January 2026; “DGISPR tells Afghan Taliban regime to choose between terrorist organisations and Pakistan”, Dawn , 27 February 2026. Islamabad’s public response has been to highlight Indian human rights violations in Kashmir in international forums, including at the UN Security Council, calling New Delhi out for what it calls “state-sponsored” terrorism against Kashmiri Muslims. 102 “UNSC condemns Swat suicide blast after Pakistan sounds alarm on Afghan terrorist havens”, Dawn , 6 June 2026. In an implied reference to Indian-administered Kashmir, it has also demanded a clear “distinction between terrorism and the legitimate struggle against foreign occupation and the right of self-determination”. 103 “Pakistan calls for internal reform of UN’s counterterrorism architecture”, Dawn , 2 July 2026. Islamabad has gone on to accuse New Delhi of “weaponising” water, warning that it would have no choice but to act, including militarily, should India store or divert waters allocated to Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty. 104 The three western rivers allocated to Pakistan under the treaty supply 80 per cent of the country’s total water consumption. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan, Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Despite the rhetoric, the Kashmir dispute appears to have lost much of its prominence in Pakistan as Islamabad’s attention shifts from its South Asian neighbourhood to the Middle East. In September 2025, Pakistan signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia, cementing a longstanding partnership; it went on to sign a joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye the following August. Islamabad has also assumed the mantle of mediator since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, leveraging its strategic and diplomatic links with the U.S., as well as its working relationship with neighbouring Iran. 105 Crisis Group Commentary, “Pakistan: A New Player in the Quest for a U.S.-Iran Breakthrough”, 4 June 2026. As a result, Pakistan would appear to have few incentives and little need to meddle in India, let alone support Islamist jihadist proxies in Kashmir, according to one Pakistani analyst. Pakistani policymakers are said to be well aware that backing a proxy war would corroborate the BJP government’s portrayal of Pakistan as a threat to regional stability and global peace. 106 Crisis Group telephone interview, August 2026. Another prominent Pakistani analyst, however, warned that even the “creeping presence” of anti-India jihadist groups, particularly Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, should be a matter of concern for Islamabad. So long as the authorities do not rigorously enforce the ban on such groups, India’s claims will not ring hollow. 107 Mohammad Amir Rana, “A New Pakistan”, Dawn , 13 July 2025. C. The Delhi Blast and the Threat of Religious Violence On 10 November 2025, a car laden with explosives blew up at a busy intersection in New Delhi, killing fifteen and injuring more than 30 people. 108 “Delhi car blast: Doctors with bombs”, The Hindu , 18 November 2025. The driver, who died in the blast, turned out to be a Kashmiri doctor, seemingly adding a new dimension to conflict in the region. Investigative agencies claim to have uncovered a “white-collar terror” network, including five other physicians from Kashmir; in all, thirteen individuals have been accused of belonging to it so far, including a woman doctor from the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. All Muslim, they were allegedly attempting to revive Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind, an offshoot of al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent. 109 Al-Qaeda’s influence on Kashmiri militancy has been minimal, as Kashmiris consider the group’s ideology too extreme. The presence of a local separatist leadership also reduced the pull of transnational jihadism. Given the Kashmir links, Indian security agencies carried out an extensive crackdown in the Himalayan region, demolishing the suspects’ houses in the process. Despite Prime Minister Modi’s earlier threat to retaliate against Pakistan for every terrorist attack perpetrated in India, the government refrained from immediately blaming Islamabad, possibly out of desire to avoid another war. In the end, the National Investigative Agency concluded the attack was carried out by a group led by medical professionals and inspired by the al-Qaeda splinter rather than Pakistan-backed militants. 110 According to the NIA, the accused formed Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind Interim in June 2022, after a failed attempt to travel to Afghanistan, stockpiling arms and ammunition as well as manufacturing explosives using commercially available chemicals. “NIA names three more accused in supplementary chargesheet in Red Fort area blast case”, The Hindu , 27 June 2026. The involvement of physicians in a suicide bombing came as a shock to Kashmiri society. Though militants have carried out suicide attacks in Kashmir in the past and educated individuals have become insurgents, these two trends have rarely overlapped. For now, the attack remains a one-off event, with no evidence that it forms part of a larger trend. That said, it has raised alarm in Kashmir at the prospect that more suicide bomb cells made up of young people may emerge. Though the New Delhi bombers had not previously been jailed, some Kashmiris are concerned that young adults incarcerated under anti-terror laws are being exposed to the influence of hard-core militants and separatist ideologues, and often turn to religion to cope with jail life. 111 Crisis Group interview, Waheed Ur Rehman Para, member of Legislative Assembly, Srinagar, November 2025. Meanwhile, the permanent fear of state surveillance appears to have played a central role in the breakdown of social cohesion and communication in the traditionally close-knit Kashmiri community. 112 “Radicalisation in Kashmir: The ideological transformation”, The New Indian Express , 16 November 2025. “I no longer know how my son thinks or whether he knows about his son”, a former Kashmiri bureaucrat noted, lamenting the fraying of bonds in society. 113 Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. Investigative agencies claimed that a group of medical professionals from Kashmir was responsible for a suicide blast in New Delhi last November, killing fifteen and injuring many more. Koil, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi Two of the doctors were from Koil village in South Kashmir whose homes were demolished by the security forces. Koli, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi V. A Way Forward It is becoming increasingly clear that India’s efforts to revamp Kashmir by stamping out resistance and establishing central control of its administration have failed. New Delhi should turn the page by recognising the political dispute at the heart of the region’s unrest, eschewing the temptation to view all militancy through a religious lens and reorienting its approach through a series of steps that would allow it to manage the conflict more effectively. A. Restoring Political Rights Though several indicators of unrest in Jammu and Kashmir have steadily declined, including militant violence, street demonstrations and stone throwing, the region is at constant risk of renewed turbulence. Trying to build stability on a foundation of central rule, heavy-handed law enforcement and counter-insurgency is not the right approach. Despite the BJP government’s claims to the contrary, Kashmiri Muslims believe that the changes imposed since 2019 have been motivated by prejudice in the shape of a Hindu nationalist desire to disenfranchise them. As the 2024 elections show, diverse and hitherto antagonistic political forces in Kashmir, from mainstream politicians to separatists, have come together in response to the perceived threat to the region’s community and way of life. Tacit support for militant groups has also grown among a number of Kashmiris, who have come to think that armed struggle is the only way to prevent India from overhauling the region’s socio-religious identity and robbing it of political autonomy. A continued campaign of militant violence, however, is likely to aggravate tensions with New Delhi and fuel bilateral discord between India and Pakistan, stoking instability that is not in the interests of India’s rulers, the Kashmiri people or the rest of South Asia. To avert these risks, it is vital that New Delhi devise an approach to address the wellsprings of public disaffection in the region. New Delhi should first and foremost seek to rebuild a basis of public trust in the region. That should begin with restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, a step Prime Minister Modi himself has promised to take on several occasions. Though the move would be insufficient to quell all of Kashmiris’ grievances, it would at least remove one source of resentment. Making the chief minister subordinate to the New Delhi appointed lieutenant governor has been widely perceived as a humiliation. Reversing it would, to an extent, help win back Kashmir’s disillusioned pro-India political factions and could help weaken public sympathy for militancy. A decision on the issue nevertheless appears to have been delayed due to the government’s lack of confidence in security conditions following the Pahalgam attack. 114 The head BJP member of Jammu and Kashmir’s legislature said statehood will be restored when the security situation is under control. See “Statehood to J&K only after end to violence against youth, children: BJP’s Sunil Sharma”, PTI, 5 February 2026. More broadly, New Delhi prefers to maintain a firm grip on the region for a couple of reasons: it does not trust regional political forces to tackle militancy, and it seeks to build national political capital by proving it can control violence in Kashmir. Its current approach, however, is self-defeating. In the words of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, there are “two parallel governments running the same territory”, with the lieutenant governor granted greater powers, especially in matters of public safety. 115 “ The Economic Times : ‘UT with an assembly is the worst form of government’: Omar Abdullah says two govts in J&K can’t work”, video, YouTube, 18 June 2025. Abdullah and other observers note that despite its prerogatives, the administration under the lieutenant governor lacks the grassroots networks needed to track militancy and prevent future attacks. 116 Crisis Group interviews, Srinagar, November 2025. See also “I take full responsibility: J&K LG Manoj Sinha calls Pahalgam attack a security failure”, Times of India , 14 July 2025. Restoring statehood would ... serve New Delhi’s longstanding goal of achieving greater participation by Kashmiris in India’s democracy. Restoring statehood would also serve New Delhi’s longstanding goal of achieving greater participation by Kashmiris in India’s democracy. For Kashmiris, the image of a disempowered government fosters the perception that voting in elections is futile. The two elections conducted after the change in the region’s status certainly recorded high voter turnout, with even separatists abstaining from their usual boycott calls. Even so, many voters cast their ballots to vent their frustration with New Delhi’s decisions and to keep the BJP at bay, rather than out of conviction that the outcome would make any material change. It was precisely disillusionment with Indian democracy that triggered the first major surge in militant violence in 1989. 117 New Delhi’s rigging of the 1987 regional polls was the trigger for the separatist insurgency that erupted in 1989, with many candidates who had been jailed turning to militancy upon their release. See Praveen Donthi, “ Kashmir Votes to Repudiate Rule from the Centre ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 October 2024. If restoring statehood is not feasible for political or security reasons in the short term, the central government should consider restoring some of the chief minister’s powers in the interim, with a degree of oversight by the lieutenant governor. The chief minister should, at the very least, have the power to appoint civil servants, one of the post’s main functions in all other Indian states and Union territories. The chief minister’s command of the police should also be restored, albeit by increments. Blocking the chief minister’s office from handling the threat of militancy is counterproductive, as security forces working alone cannot properly track local insurgent activity in a complex and evolving conflict. B. Loosening the Iron Grip The government’s determination to claim it has pacified Kashmir places immense pressure on security forces to live up to that expectation, resulting in the widespread use of draconian anti-terror laws against local people suspected of having militant links. But this approach has tended to fuel resentment of the Indian state, even spurring some of those marked for arrest to join or lend support to militant groups. 118 Crisis Group observations, Jammu and Kashmir, 2021-2025. See also “Youth share tales of harassment at PDP meet on why Kashmiri professionals are turning to violence”, The Hindu , 8 December 2025. Measures such as demolishing the homes of suspected militants’ families without investigation increase the collective sense of victimhood. So does dismissing government employees on mere suspicion of ties to insurgents. Given the consequences for those on the receiving end, New Delhi should stop applying its anti-terror laws so broadly. As an official admitted: “It’s better to make an example out of a handful of guilty people than to resort to collective punishment, which will backfire”. 119 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Srinagar, 2024. Kashmiri observers have also voiced growing concern about rising radicalism and religious fundamentalism among the region’s young people, particularly among those arrested under the anti-terror laws who have come to embrace an extremist version of Islam as a way to cope with imprisonment. 120 Kashmiri observers point out that the government’s practice of transferring detained young Kashmiris to prisons outside the region, where most of the inmates are Hindu, is further pushing them to embrace religion. Crisis Group interview, Waheed Ur Rehman Para, member of Legislative Assembly, Srinagar, November 2025. The case of the young Kashmiri doctors who carried out the 2025 New Delhi blast suggests the problem extends beyond those in jail. 121 A Kashmiri legislator said the blast was not just a political act of terror but also had radical religious undertones. Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, November 2025. In private, security officials voice regret that New Delhi is solely focused on eliminating militants, while doing little to create conditions that discourage them or weaken their cause. 122 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Kashmir, 2025. The use of harsh anti-terror laws for minor transgressions such as posts on social media stands out as particularly counterproductive, as does blacklisting young people who have been charged with disturbing law and order when they later apply for government jobs. 123 “J&K cops to deny security clearance to stone pelters for passport, govt jobs”, The Indian Express , 2 August 2021. C. India-Pakistan: Dialogue amid Distrust New Delhi shows little appetite for engagement with Islamabad given the terrorist attacks perpetrated on its territory, for which it has blamed its neighbour. While Islamabad has officially banned the jihadist groups Lashkar-e-Tayyeba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, which are allegedly responsible for many attacks, they have often re-emerged under changed names, including through charity and political fronts. While these too are proscribed, the groups still seem able to revive themselves, prompting New Delhi to accuse Pakistan of failing to take action against them. 124 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. If it is to convince India that its efforts are genuine, Pakistan will need to aggressively enforce its ban on anti-Indian jihadist groups. India, for its part, should rethink its stance that Operation Sindoor has only been paused, as Modi has put it, implying that military action could immediately resume if another terrorist attack occurs. 125 Ibid. While this novel approach is meant to boost India’s deterrence, it puts India on a perpetual war footing and increases the risk of conflict with Pakistan, the consequences of which could be calamitous. 126 Ibid. Kashmiri militants, whether local or foreign, could well aim to conduct another terror attack on Indian soil. 127 The U.S. Directorate of National Intelligence assessed in its 2026 report that “conditions exist for terrorist actors to continue to create catalysts for crises”. See “Annual Threat Assessment of the US Intelligence Community”, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, March 2026, p. 24. For some observers, the next India-Pakistan conflict is thus “a question of when, not if”. 128 “In West Asia, a widening conflict with no clear ends”, Hindustan Times , 7 March 2026; “The faint hope for peace between India and Pakistan”, Time , 26 June 2026. It is true that, despite its combative posture and promises to retaliate against all attacks, the Indian government has proven more cautious than expected, taking great care not to blame Pakistan after the November 2025 New Delhi blast. But whether it can withstand domestic pressure in the event of another large-scale attack is hard to predict. In these circumstances, resuming a modicum of dialogue with Islamabad has taken on extra urgency. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has ... turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. New Delhi has thus far rebuffed Pakistan’s diplomatic overtures, including the Pakistani prime minister’s offer of dialogue to settle contentious issues, from terrorism to disputes over water sharing and the fate of Jammu and Kashmir. 129 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “PM urges India to ‘hold’ meaningful dialogue on Kashmir”, The News , 5 February 2025. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has also turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. 130 Maleeha Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, Dawn , 15 June 2026. The two sides have reportedly participated in a few discreet Track 1.5 and 2 dialogues, unofficial discussions held by former officials and experts who are not representatives of any state. 131 “India Pakistan held Track 1.5, 2 meetings after Operation Sindoor”, Hindustan Times , 17 April 2026. As a former senior Pakistani diplomat noted, however, such exchanges have limited value since participants seldom deviate from the stated positions of their home countries. 132 Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, op. cit. Signs of greater inclination to engage with Islamabad have nevertheless begun to emerge on the Indian side. A senior leader from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the BJP’s powerful parent organisation, has for the first time spoken up about the need to engage with Pakistan, arguing that while India has every right to “respond appropriately” to terror incidents backed by Islamabad, it should leave the door to dialogue open. 133 “Why has the RSS called for dialogue with Pakistan?”, The Hindu , 17 May 2026; “‘India should not close doors for dialogue with Pakistan’: RSS general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale”, Times of India , 12 May 2026. Given the RSS’s influence, this stance could help assuage public hostility to diplomacy with Pakistan. 134 The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (the National Volunteers Association, or RSS) is a Hindu nationalist organisation founded in 1925, of which the BJP is just one of many wings. With millions of members, it is considered the largest NGO in the world. For a critical view of the RSS, see “Mamdani opposes NYC event with leader of India’s Hindu nationalist group”, Reuters, 26 August 2026. Islamabad has reacted cautiously to the RSS call, with the foreign ministry waiting to see if its views reflect India’s official policy. 135 “FO waiting to see how India reacts to ‘pro-dialogue chorus”, Dawn , 15 May 2026. Few in Pakistan, however, are optimistic regarding the revival of formal talks with India so long as the BJP government continues to accuse the country of supporting jihadist groups and fighting a proxy war with its neighbour. 136 Crisis Group telephone interviews, August 2026. See also Touqir Hussain, “Modi’s Pakistan policy”, Dawn , 13 August 2026. Hussain is a former Pakistan ambassador. The absence of direct lines of communication beyond military-to-military channels increases conflict risks, including as the result of miscalculation or misunderstanding. Despite abiding distrust of its neighbour, India has, in the past, maintained communication through back channels with Pakistan, even in times of crisis. 137 The prime ministers of India and Pakistan spoke to each other even at the height of the Kargil conflict of 1999, for example, and the two national security advisers have been in regular touch during other tense episodes. At present, however, the only communication channel in place is a hotline between the directors general of military operations. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “India and Pakistan: Neighbours who do not talk to each other”, The India Forum , 10 April 2026. Since there are few prospects for formal talks between India and Pakistan’s top leaders, behind-the-scenes diplomacy could play a vital role in defusing the threat of fresh clashes. Such quiet contacts could enable political leaders to communicate, if not directly, then at least through their national security advisers. 138 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Reviving such a mechanism would allow both sides to communicate their red lines and, perhaps most importantly, avoid misunderstanding or misinterpretation of the other’s actions. They should establish this bilateral channel outside the limelight to avoid the domestic pressures both might face should news of it leak. At the same time, Indian authorities could make it clear to the public that any level of engagement would not amount to normalising relations or offering concessions to Islamabad, including over its territorial claims on Kashmir. Authorities in Islamabad could also assure the Pakistani public that Pakistan’s position on Kashmir’s disputed status or other contentious issues such as the country’s rights under the Indus Waters Treaty would not be compromised. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both [India and Pakistan] to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Even then, back-channel diplomacy is unlikely to make much headway if the Indian and Pakistani governments succumb to the temptation of nationalist outbursts and tit-for-tat allegations against each other. A tentative diplomatic opening is also likely to fail if Pakistan does not address India’s suspicions of continued support for anti-India jihadist groups more robustly. It is in Islamabad’s interest to rigorously enforce the law banning all jihadist entities. In return, Islamabad will expect New Delhi to respond to its concerns about alleged Indian backing for anti-Pakistan Baloch militant groups and the Pakistani Taliban. Progress in reducing mutual trust on such contentious issues is unlikely to happen overnight. But a high-level back channel between the national security advisers could still play an important role in this respect. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Foreign governments that enjoy friendly relations with both parties, such as the U.S., the UK, EU member states, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries, can also help stabilise the relationship. Considering India’s sensitivities regarding foreign interference or mediation on the Kashmir issue, external powers should move cautiously with quiet, behind-the-scenes diplomacy. They should emphasise that it is in New Delhi and Islamabad’s mutual interest to ensure a sustainable peace in South Asia, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse potential conflict triggers. After seven years, the tough security measures and federal rule have not only failed to bring peace but may also have fostered support for militant groups in some circles. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi VI. Conclusion Seven years after the Indian government revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s special autonomous status, redrew its boundaries, overhauled its administrative set-up and undertook numerous reforms ostensibly to foster peace, the threats to local and regional security from the restive Himalayan region persist – and have arguably grown more serious given their impact on relations with Pakistan. Though the government has succeeded in reducing conflict-related violence, the stringent measures it has employed to do so and the threat it has posed to Kashmiris’ sense of identity are fuelling deep discontent. New Delhi’s efforts to impose central rule appear not to have achieved their goal of eradicating militancy. They may even have fostered support in some circles for insurgent groups. If it is to achieve a durable peace in Jammu and Kashmir, India should address as a priority Kashmiris’ growing disaffection. Ideally, that would start by honouring the promise to restore the region’s statehood, paving the way to reinstatement of a democratically elected regional government with real power. New Delhi should also review its tactics in combating militant groups, particularly by being more discriminating in the way it applies its anti-terror laws. Sparked by a terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, the brief but intense clashes between India and Pakistan in 2025 were a stark reminder of how devastating this oft-forgotten dispute could be if it gets out of hand.
