Resumption of some form of dialogue between the two nuclear neighbours is essential, preferably through a discreet back channel. With its aspirations for a “New Kashmir” proving overly optimistic, the Indian government should do more to ensure that this unresolved conflict does not become the trigger for far greater harm. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/23/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 23 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 23 October 2026 CUBA The UN General Assembly will vote next week on its annual resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba, in place for more than six decades. Last year’s resolution passed 165-7. Washington is seeking to reduce the resolution’s backing as the Trump administration pursues a broader economic pressure campaign on the island (including restrictions on oil shipments and new secondary sanctions). U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents, who argued that supporting the resolution excuses the Cuban government’s human rights abuses while obscuring its role in the country’s economic crisis. Cuban diplomats denounced the panel as an attempt to deflect attention from the embargo’s effects. Crisis Group expert Michael Bustamante says the confrontation illustrates the unfortunate either-or terms in which the debate is often framed. Decrying the humanitarian consequences of U.S. measures need not mean absolving the Cuban government of responsibility for its economic policy failures or its suppression of dissent. STRAIT OF HORMUZ October has already seen Iran hit more ships in or around the Strait of Hormuz than any previous month of the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February. Tehran’s escalation comes after the volume of crude oil moving through the strait reached pre-war levels, largely through a scheme by which a few risk-tolerant tankers are assuming the danger of hauling barrels through the waterway before transferring their cargo to more risk-averse vessels outside it. Crisis Group expert Chris Newton says the question now is whether Iran can make these “shuttle runs” too costly. If it cannot, it will lose leverage in any negotiations with the U.S. and Gulf Arab countries that may transpire. But if it can, its attacks could prompt retaliatory U.S. strikes. U.S. - UKRAINE Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that U.S. intelligence sharing, crucial for advance warning of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, had been restored. At the same time, there were conflicting reports on a slowdown in Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite system, which it depends on for battlefield communications and defensive drones. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “throttling” of Starlink, which is run by billionaire Elon Musk's company SpaceX, was a technical error that “no one ordered”. The incident nonetheless fuelled speculation that the Trump administration is scaling back intelligence and technological support for Ukraine to strong-arm Kyiv into making concessions to Moscow ahead of the 3 November U.S. midterm elections. Wednesday’s meeting between Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian”, has done the same. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Zelenskyy’s resistance to U.S. pressure has boosted his approval ratings at home. Polls show that a majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding territory in return for a peace settlement. 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing says survivor services are increasingly scarce after major U.S. aid cuts in 2025 hit programming for which Washington had been the largest donor. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. Though the policy’s ban on “promoting” abortion exempts cases of rape, many NGOs fear inconsistent enforcement and unclear compliance requirements, leaving them to choose between U.S. conditions that may limit post-rape care and refusing funding at the risk of jeopardising their wider operations. LEBANON Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. The deal follows a severe Israeli escalation, including its deepest incursion into Lebanese territory in 26 years, which threatened to upset ongoing U.S.-Iran talks. The ceasefire depends on Hizbollah halting attacks and withdrawing fighters from south of the Litani River to allow the Lebanese army to assume control there. On Thursday, Hizbollah rejected the terms, after Israel said it would continue military operations for now. He was upbeat, releasing a fifteen-point “roadmap” for the next stage. But conditions remain dire on the ground. Israel’s siege is tightening, meaning that reconstruction is impossible. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday he has ordered the Israeli army to increase the proportion of Gaza it controls from 60 to 70 per cent, in effect squeezing the strip’s two million people into an even tighter corner. Israeli airstrikes have taken more than 900 Palestinian lives during the ceasefire, including the commander of Hamas’s armed wing and, only days later, his successor, who was killed Wednesday along with his family. Israeli media reported that the Board of Peace had “approved” the assassinations. Crisis Group expert Max Rodenbeck says the Board’s strategy of making relief for Gaza’s people, whether humanitarian aid or broader hopes for the future, conditional on Hamas’s willingness to surrender its arms is deeply troubling and a recipe for prolonging their misery. KOREAN PENINSULA Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. The same day, Seoul said it had also detected North Korean missile launches toward waters off the peninsula’s western coast. Crisis Group expert Chris Green says the advanced weapon tests will deepen the freeze in peninsular relations, with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un branding South Korea his country’s foremost enemy and pledging to make the border “an impregnable fortress”. Along with Pyongyang’s growing closeness to Moscow and questions about Washington’s commitment to defending South Korea amid its mounting competition with Beijing, the tests are likely to bolster the consensus in Seoul behind more intensive military modernisation of its own. MALI As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). Meanwhile, JNIM continued to enforce a partial siege of the capital Bamako, preventing scores of trucks bearing fuel and other supplies from reaching the city. In the north, Malian forces have stepped up airstrikes on Kidal and surrounding areas following the major offensive launched on 25 April by JNIM and northern separatist groups. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says these developments show that weapons continue to do the talking in Mali, even as the situation points to the urgent need for a genuine political dialogue. 22 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN Together with various NGOs, the UN released a plan Tuesday for aiding Afghan refugees expected to return from Iran and Pakistan in the coming months. The UN projects that 2.7 million people will cross back into Afghanistan between April and December. Already, nearly 5.9 million refugees have come back since September 2023, many of them forced to do so by harsh Pakistani visa policies amid rising tensions between Islamabad and the Taliban authorities in Kabul. Now the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will likely compel many Afghans living in the Islamic Republic to leave, even as the exodus from Pakistan continues. Many of these people are women, who will face draconian Taliban restrictions on freedom of movement and economic activity. The returnees also include children, some of whom have never even been to Afghanistan and will be at greater risk of child marriage, which the Taliban have lately recognised as a legal act. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says international donors should give generously to fund the $529 million UN response plan, without which many returnees will be destitute. NIGERIA The military announced Tuesday that joint strikes carried out with the U.S. had killed 175 jihadist fighters in the preceding week, in addition to destroying stockpiles of arms. The strikes began on 16 May with one that killed Abu Bakr al-Mainuki, deputy leader of the Islamic State-West Africa Province (ISWAP), who had been coordinating activities with jihadists in the Sahelian countries. At a hearing in Washington on Tuesday, General Dagvin Anderson, head of U.S. Africa Command, told U.S. legislators that “the epicentre of global terrorism is in Africa”. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest operations underscore that Nigerian-U.S. security cooperation is deeper than Abuja and Washington had indicated earlier. They are a setback for ISWAP, at least for the time being. U.S. - CUBA The U.S. indicted former Cuban leader Raúl Castro Wednesday for murder and conspiring to kill U.S. nationals. The charges relate to a 1996 incident in which Cuban fighter jets shot at planes flown by anti-Castro Cuban Americans trying to help Cubans escape the island. These legal developments arrive amid renewed speculation that the Trump administration intends to decapitate the Cuban regime much as it did the Venezuelan government with its raid to snatch former President Nicolás Maduro in early January. Senior U.S. officials, most recently Central Intelligence Agency head John Ratcliffe, have held a series of semi-secret meetings with high-ranking figures in Havana this spring. Publicly, Cuban leader Miguel Díaz-Canel has remained defiant, rejecting the allegations against Castro as a “political manoeuvre”. Meanwhile, the U.S. has tightened a blockade of Cuba that has precipitated a humanitarian crisis and sent additional warships to the Caribbean Sea. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says any attempt to forcibly break the tight grip the Cuban Communist Party and military have upon the state could result in violent chaos and further suffering for the Cuban people. 15 May 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO A spate of lethal violence in the north-eastern Ituri province over the past two weeks has underscored the complexity of the country’s crisis. In late April, a group of Codeco militiamen killed at least 69 people, mainly civilians, in a series of separate attacks. Allied with the Congolese government, Codeco claims to defend the interests of the Lendu people, most of whom are farmers, from encroachment by ethnic Hema herders. According to local sources, it raided several Hema villages in retaliation for assaults on Congolese army positions by a Hema armed group. The following week, gunmen from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), a Ugandan insurgency now affiliated with the Islamic State, killed at least fifteen people in Biakato, an Ituri market town. The province has been under martial law since 2021, the same year that Uganda (with Kinshasa’s permission) sent in troops to pursue ADF militants based in Congolese territory. Crisis Group expert Onesphore Sematumba says the latest killings demonstrate the inadequacy of a purely military response to insecurity stemming from inter-communal tensions, competition for natural resources, state weakness and other causes. DISPLACEMENT A new report from the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre shows that armed conflict has become the number-one cause of internal displacement worldwide, surpassing natural disasters, for the first time on record. War and violence drove some 32.3 million people from their homes in 2025, the most ever, representing a 60 per cent increase over 2024. The internal displacements in Iran and the Democratic Republic of Congo made up two thirds of the global total. Crisis Group President and CEO Comfort Ero says these numbers are a sobering reminder of how pervasive conflict has become in today’s world. The human cost of war is never abstract. Preventing war means not just saving lives but also sparing people the pain and distress of being uprooted, often with no certainty of ever going home. U.S. - CHINA U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded their long-awaited summit Friday. Crisis Group experts Ali Wyne and William Yang say it produced no major breakthrough, such as a joint commitment to de-escalate the conflict in the Middle East and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Nor did it bring a major reversal, which some in Taiwan had feared, such as Trump agreeing to scale back U.S. arms sales or change Washington’s longstanding declaratory policies toward the island. The summit was nonetheless illuminating in two respects. First, it underscored Trump’s desire to gain a greater foothold in China for U.S. businesses as well as his conviction that a strong working rapport with Xi can produce a cooperative relationship between Washington and Beijing. Secondly, it showcased how significantly China’s power and confidence have grown since Trump last visited China in November 2017. 8 May 2026 CAMBODIA - THAILAND The Thai cabinet voted Tuesday to cancel a 2001 memorandum of understanding with Cambodia on overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand. Yet, in the 25 years since they signed it, the two countries have neither undertaken such projects nor resolved their territorial dispute. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, who campaigned on scrapping the document arguing that it had failed to achieve its objectives, insists that the decision is unrelated to tensions with Cambodia following border clashes in 2025. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says the cancellation will please Thai nationalists who have long alleged that the agreement placed Bangkok at a disadvantage, despite its language saying it is “without prejudice to the maritime claims of either party”. Cambodia expressed regret at Thailand’s action and said it plans to initiate compulsory conciliation, a non-binding dispute resolution mechanism under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. ETHIOPIA A showdown may be looming in Tigray, Ethiopia’s northernmost region, after its ruling party reinstated a state council Tuesday that was dissolved immediately before the bloody 2020-2022 Tigray war. The council was originally elected in 2020, in defiance of the federal government’s wishes. Addis Ababa installed a regional administration of its own choosing following the war, which Tigray’s ruling party has now, in effect, deposed. All eyes are now on the federal government, says Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor, watching for how it will respond. It has already imposed what amounts to an economic siege on Tigray, blocking fuel supplies and withholding budget subsidies. It may simply tighten these measures. Or it may intervene militarily to reinstate an Addis Ababa-aligned administration. U.S. - CHINA Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to host U.S. President Donald Trump in Beijing next week for a long-awaited summit, which had been slated for the end of March. Crisis Group experts Ali Wyne and William Yang say trade will likely feature high on the agenda, with both men aiming to maintain the tariff truce they reached last year. The Middle East conflict – which caused the delay – will also loom large, and both will seek to use it for leverage. The U.S. has sanctioned five Chinese oil refiners and accused China of “funding the largest state sponsor of terrorism” as it maintains a naval blockade of Iran. But Washington needs Chinese gallium to replenish its stockpile of missile interceptors in the Middle East, and it may need Beijing’s help to get Tehran back to the negotiating table. In exchange, Xi may try to extract security concessions from Trump, perhaps by asking him to lessen U.S. defence backing for Taiwan or to declare that the U.S. “opposes“ (rather than “does not support“, which is the longstanding U.S. position) Taiwanese independence. 1 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Fresh violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan erupted this week. Afghan authorities said Pakistani mortars and missiles hit a university and residential neighbourhoods in eastern Kunar province on Monday, killing at least seven people and wounding at least 85. Pakistan denied targeting civilians, saying its strikes aimed at militants, based on intelligence. The exchanges followed China-mediated talks in April, during which the two sides agreed to explore a diplomatic solution to their dispute. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says mutual partners, particularly China, should urge both sides to de-escalate tensions, including through an agreed-upon oversight mechanism, to prevent the situation from deteriorating further. COLOMBIA Nearly two dozen people are dead and scores injured after a series of apparently coordinated attacks in the country’s south west that authorities blamed on Estado Mayor Central (EMC), a dissident faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. Militants used drones, explosives and roadblocks to hit targets including police stations and military bases. On 25 April, improvised explosive devices went off on a major highway in Cauca, striking a bus and other civilian vehicles, killing at least twenty. The preceding a day, a bus full of explosives detonated near a major military base in Cali, Colombia's third-largest city. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the wave of violence indicates EMC’s capacity to disrupt daily life and terrorise civilians. Colombia's next president, to be elected on 31 May, will need to take urgent steps to better protect civilians. MALI On Saturday, the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, alongside separatists from the Azawad Liberation Front in northern Mali, assailed seven Malian cities, including the capital Bamako. Militants struck the garrison at Kati, less than 20km from Bamako, often described as the centre of military power, where they assassinated the defence minister and reportedly wounded other regime figures. They also retook the northern city of Kidal, the symbolic seat of the separatist movement, before negotiating the departure of Russian paramilitaries and Malian troops. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jézéquel says these attacks mark a new stage in Mali’s decades-long jihadist insurgency, characterised by increased pressure on urban areas, aimed at weakening and delegitimising state authority. 24 April 2026 JAPAN On Monday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet lifted restrictions on the export of lethal weapons, allowing Japan to sell arms to seventeen countries with which it has defence transfer agreements. Tokyo first limited such transactions in 1967 and instituted a near total ban in 1976. It will continue to bar arms exports to countries at war, but exceptions may be granted. Meanwhile, last Saturday Beijing said two Chinese navy ships had transited waters between Japan’s Amami Oshima and Yokoate islands for exercises in the western Pacific. The announcement came one day before Japanese combat troops joined the annual Philippine-U.S. Balikatan exercise for the first time. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says these developments illustrate the accelerating defence modernisation in the Asia Pacific in response to what U.S.-allied countries perceive as Beijing’s coercive behaviour and uncertainty about Washington’s ability to sustain strategic focus on the region. ROHINGYA Nearly 900 Rohingya refugees died or were reported missing while trying to make perilous sea crossings in 2025, the UN said last week. It is the highest number ever, representing one in seven of the Rohingya who braved such journeys. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says this grim record points to the increasing desperation among the Rohingya in camps in southern Bangladesh, who are facing cuts to food aid. Unable to go home to Myanmar’s Rakhine State, which is wracked by war, or to work legally in Bangladesh, ever more refugees are trying to escape by boat to Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia. The new Bangladeshi government should permit Rohingya to secure jobs in sectors with labour shortages. The more ways the Rohingya have to earn a living in refuge, the fewer of them will risk their lives at sea. U.S. - IRAN President Donald Trump announced an indefinite extension of the ceasefire in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran Tuesday, though keeping the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports in place. Iran tightened its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz Wednesday, firing on two cargo vessels attempting passage. Negotiations in Pakistan seem to be on hold, with conflicting signals about whether Tehran will send a delegation. With major combat on pause, say Crisis Group experts Michael Wahid Hanna and Ali Vaez, both sides are seeking to gain the upper hand through economic disruption – Washington by tightening its financial squeeze on the Islamic Republic and Tehran by prolonging the uncertainty in global markets. Meanwhile, it adds yet another impediment to resuming talks. 17 April 2026 LIBYA The rival Tripoli and Benghazi-based legislative bodies approved a U.S.-mediated unified budget Saturday. The first such budget in more than thirteen years, it consolidates public spending throughout the country within a single framework. SOUTH SUDAN Opposition forces this week retook the strategic town of Akobo in Jonglei state after government troops withdrew. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region mloukili Fri, 10/23/2026 - 10:58 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Algeria's President Abdelmadjid Tebboune (L) speaks with United Arab Emirates’ President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan as they pose for a photo during the G7 Summit hosted by Italy, in Savelletri, on 14 June, 2024. AFP / Ludovic Marin Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 23 October 2026 13 minutes How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region Algiers has severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi, following years of discord over crises in North Africa and the Sahel. The two countries see their dispute very differently, but it has nonetheless become a rivalry that could put regional stability at risk. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Michaël Béchir Ayari Senior Analyst, Tunisia Related Tags Algeria United Arab Emirates On 10 September, Algeria broke off diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, in the latest manifestation of a confrontation between the two countries over policy in the Middle East, North Africa and the Sahel. Since 2020, disagreements have festered between Algiers and Abu Dhabi over Israel, Morocco and Western Sahara. Algeria has also grown increasingly suspicious of the aims of Emirati involvement in crises in Libya, Sudan and Sahelian states. The rupture is marked by an asymmetry of perceptions. Algiers sees the UAE, sitting far away in the Gulf, as interfering in its North African and Sahelian neighbourhood, where it is looking to rebuild the diplomatic clout that it wielded for decades after winning independence from French colonial rule in 1962. It views Emirati interventions as, at the very least, encroachments upon its historical domain. Abu Dhabi, for its part, says economic ties, not Algeria, are central to its African engagement. It forswears any intent to provoke or sideline Algiers. The bilateral discord has become a full-blown rivalry, however, and one that is becoming perilous as regional security arrangements are changing. Algeria is forging closer links with Niger, as well as with Chad. It is also backing the Sudanese army in its war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in its power struggle with Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, whose forces control the country’s east . Algerian officials describe these moves as reinforcing the country’s “ strategic borders ”. Algeria remains bitterly at odds with Morocco over Western Sahara and other issues, and it is just now repairing relations with Mali. Meanwhile, the UAE is forming its own partnerships in North Africa and the Sahel, which can involve both states and armed groups, and which often (though not always) put it indirectly in competition with Algeria. A direct clash between the two countries is unlikely. Their respective alliance systems overlap somewhat and do not constitute coherent groups of adversaries. Still, jostling among them could draw in Algeria, the UAE or both, with the risk of local escalation or inadvertent confrontation. Roots of the Break-up Dramatic as the 10 September rupture was, it had been a long time coming. Until 2020, relations between Algeria and the UAE were strong. In the early 1970s, Algeria sent oil experts, including executives from Sonatrach, Algeria’s state-owned hydrocarbons company, to the Gulf to help establish the institutions that would become the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. Abdelaziz Bouteflika, who served as Algeria’s president between 1999 and 2019, lived in Abu Dhabi from 1984 to 1987, working as a diplomatic adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, father of today’s leader Mohammed bin Zayed (aka MBZ). During Bouteflika’s tenure as Algerian head of state, Emirati capital made significant inroads into the Algerian economy, including in the defence sector. In 2012, for example, Emirati investors cooperated with the Algerian defence ministry and state-owned companies in joint ventures to produce Mercedes-Benz vehicles and Emirati-designed NIMR armoured vehicles in Algeria. The UAE built networks of contacts within the Algerian political, business and military elite, some of which survived Bouteflika’s fall in 2019. The UAE’s 2020 normalisation with Israel – part of what is known as the Abraham Accords – opened a first crack in the relationship. Algiers firmly opposed any Arab state forging ties with Israel before a comprehensive settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In September 2020, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune criticised what he described as a “ rush ” ( empressement ) toward normalisation, declaring that Algeria would not be part of it. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Algerian concerns grew further when, on 4 November 2020, the UAE became the first Arab country to open a consulate in Western Sahara, establishing a diplomatic office in Laayoune, a city in the Moroccan-controlled part of the disputed territory. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Sabri Boukadoum, then Algeria’s foreign minister, questioned the move’s compatibility with international law and reaffirmed Algerian support for Sahrawi self-determination. A month later, Morocco followed the UAE in normalising relations with Israel, prompting Algerian authorities to discern an emerging UAE-Morocco-Israel alliance in their immediate vicinity. This perception was significantly reinforced in November 2021, when Morocco and Israel signed a landmark defence cooperation agreement . The agreement formalised defence ties and paved the way for cooperation in areas including intelligence and military training. Algerian authorities viewed this deepening partnership as tantamount to a direct threat , part of a regional alignment aimed at weakening their country. Algerian worries extended to allegations of foreign interference in domestic affairs. Officials accused Morocco and Israel of supporting the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylia (MAK) , an independence movement that Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021. As evidence, they pointed to the fact that Morocco’s representative at the UN had publicly argued that the Kabyle people are entitled to exercise a right to self-determination . A number of former Algerian diplomats and commentators implicated the UAE in these purported destabilisation efforts as well: a Morocco-based think-tank separately reported on contacts between MAK representatives and Emirati figures, citing sources within the Kabyle independence movement, among others. The Dispute Deepens Other regional disagreements added to the tensions. In 2020 and again in 2022 , Abu Dhabi opposed the appointment of successive Algerian foreign ministers as UN envoys to Libya, against the backdrop of Emirati support for Field Marshal Haftar, and Algeria’s closer links with the authorities in Tripoli. The UAE cited the objections of Arab states and Libyan actors, expressing their concern that Algeria, as a neighbouring country deeply involved in the conflict, could not be viewed as an impartial mediator. Another friction point surfaced in 2023, when Algerian government-aligned media attributed the failure of Algeria’s BRICS application to Emirati manoeuvring against its candidacy. Views in Algiers on how to counter the UAE’s gambits – real and perceived – may not have been entirely aligned. Some elements of the security establishment and associated media favoured a confrontational approach, while others, including figures close to former army Chief of Staff Ahmed Gaïd Salah, worried about jeopardising significant economic interests and longstanding personal connections. The exact boundaries of these contrasting viewpoints, however, remained unclear. As Emirati actions increasingly clashed with Algeria’s regional priorities and came to be perceived as national security threats , displaying restraint became more difficult. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. In 2024, he complained that wherever conflict erupted in the region , the money of an unnamed Gulf state could be found behind it; in 2025, he said Algeria enjoyed good relations with all Gulf monarchies, except one . By the following February, he was openly denouncing a “ mini-state ” that was destabilising the Arab world and the Sahel. Successive attempts to ease tensions made little headway. Former Algerian diplomats told Crisis Group that Gulf states, including Bahrain and Oman, sent emissaries to Algiers to try mediating between the two sides. They said Algeria rejected these efforts, however, and will keep doing so as long as what it regards as Emirati meddling continues. Direct contacts endured, but they failed to achieve a thaw. By February, when Algeria terminated the 2013 bilateral agreement that provided the legal framework for air travel between the two countries, the room for compromise had considerably narrowed. Rivalry in the Sahel As relations deteriorated, the dispute increasingly spilled into a contest for influence in North Africa and the Sahel. A May 2024 tour of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso by UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan raised hackles in Algeria , which has long described Mali in particular as a “brother” nation. Abu Dhabi was offering the Sahelian capitals cooperation on counter-terrorism just as Western influence was waning in the region and the new Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was opening it to new external patrons. There were other angles as well: for the UAE, security cooperation is inseparable from economic interests, particularly when it comes to natural resources; Dubai’s role in the international gold trade, including gold originating in the Sahel, gave the UAE an additional stake in regional developments. Meanwhile, Algeria’s historical ties with Bamako and the other AES capitals were reaching a nadir. Emirati officials maintain that its engagement was not aimed at supplanting Algeria. Indeed, they rarely present Algiers as a competitor when discussing the Sahel or any other African region. Rather, they say, Abu Dhabi is pursuing a broad strategy, rooted in geo-economics , designed to expand the UAE’s footprint on a continent that has gained in importance. As an Emirati businessman and former government official told Crisis Group in explaining the scope of Abu Dhabi’s ambition, “You’re either at the table or on the menu”. Algerian officials, by contrast, view the UAE’s combination of investments and partnerships with governments, business elites and armed actors as a means of undermining their country’s interests. They regard the Sahel as crucial to Algerian security, particularly since Bamako abandoned the Algeria-mediated 2015 peace agreement with armed separatists in northern Mali, whom they fear could make common cause with co-ethnics on the Algerian side of the border. Algerian concerns were heightened by allegations of ransom payments , mentioned in an August UN report and linked to the UAE by regional sources , to the jihadist group JNIM that has grabbed chunks of Malian and other Sahelian state territory. Algiers has long argued that such payments strengthen armed groups active near its frontiers. The contrast in approach and threat perceptions became particularly acute over events in Niger. Following a 2023 coup there, relations between Algiers and Niamey soured, and they worsened further in April 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers in solidarity with authorities in Bamako, with whom Algiers was then at loggerheads over the abrogated peace agreement and other issues. Bilateral ties subsequently improved, following Nigerien leader General Abdourahamane Tiani’s visit to Algiers the following February . The two countries revived their security cooperation, and Niger even helped broker the present rapprochement between Algeria and Mali. Relations with Niger ... have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Relations with Niger also have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Algeria considers Niger key to its effort to reconnect with sub-Saharan Africa through energy and trade. Its flagship project is the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline , intended to carry Nigerian gas through Niger into Algeria and onward to Europe. Here, the UAE has a competing interest: the Trans-Saharan route directly competes with Morocco’s Atlantic pipeline , which is expected to run along the West African coast and which the UAE has backed with early financing. It is against this backdrop that Algeria viewed a failed coup against Tiani on 29 August as threatening its interests. Rumours swirled in Algiers about an Emirati hand . To date, these are unsubstantiated, but they have only deepened suspicions regarding the UAE’s activities in the Sahel. Algeria responded to the coup attempt by deploying four Su-30MKA fighter jets to Niamey , accompanied by an Il-78 aerial-refuelling aircraft and an Il-76 transport plane. Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that mechanics, logistics specialists and personnel for force protection were also dispatched. Beyond sending a clear signal of support for Tiani’s government, these steps showcased Algeria’s determination to regain influence in a region where it has lost considerable ground – and where it appears to have identified the UAE as a chief antagonist. Algeria’s actions also embodied something more, again with implications for relations with the UAE: a shift away from its longstanding aversion to military operations abroad. Since independence, Algeria’s leaders have framed the country’s foreign policy around non-alignment, anti-imperialism, national sovereignty, diplomatic mediation, South-South solidarity, support for national liberation and self-determination movements, and, importantly, non-interference in other states’ domestic affairs. There have been exceptions, and Algeria has at times interpreted this last precept flexibly when it has felt that it has important interests at stake. Overall, however, reluctance to dispatch regular military forces abroad has remained a powerful institutional constraint. Only in 2020 did a constitutional amendment create a legal framework for overseas deployments. The latter still require parliamentary approval and are restricted to internationally sanctioned missions. More recently, the army’s top general Saïd Chengriha has promoted the concept that Algeria has “ strategic borders ”. Though it does not formally establish a right to military intervention in neighbouring countries, this notion expands Algeria’s security perimeter by treating instability, armed groups and trafficking networks beyond its frontiers as potential national security threats. Rivalry in North Africa and the Horn In other regional conflicts, Algeria and the UAE likewise stand on opposing sides. In Libya, Field Marshal Haftar’s forces have, over time, received extensive Emirati backing . In contrast, Algeria has stood with Tripoli (which itself has maintained tight relations with Niger). In Sudan, Algeria sides with the army, whose leaders it considers the country’s legitimate representatives; several Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that in 2025 Algiers discreetly provided the Sudanese army with equipment, including old Russian MiG-29 fighter jets and spare parts. By contrast, Abu Dhabi refers to the army-led administration as the “ Port Sudan authority ”, in reference to its erstwhile seat in Port Sudan, treating it merely as one party to the conflict; it is widely believed to be sending support to the army’s main adversary, the RSF, though the UAE denies the claim. The divergent policies toward Sudan have had wider repercussions. Eastern and southern Libya reportedly have served as logistical corridors for supplies to the RSF allegedly originating with the Emirates . Previously, much of this materiel allegedly went through eastern Chad. For its part, the UAE maintains that its activities in eastern Chad are humanitarian , particularly getting aid to Sudanese refugees. An Algerian expert told Crisis Group that policymakers in Algiers appear intent on deepening ties with N’Djamena at least in part to counterbalance what they view as Sudan-linked Emirati networks in Chad. That said, Chadian President Idriss Déby has invested considerable political capital in his relationship with the UAE, whose substantial financial support , including a $1.5 billion budget financing agreement signed in 2023, gives the latter sway that Algeria would struggle to match. The growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. These competing relationships run the risk of reinforcing regional divisions, with Field Marshal Haftar and Chad being generally close to Abu Dhabi, while Tripoli and Niger cooperate more with Algiers. Conversely, the growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. To some extent, it already has. In August 2024, for example, Haftar’s forces moved toward Ghadames, only a few kilometres from the Algerian frontier, a development Algiers saw as threatening. The crisis eventually subsided after Haftar’s spokesman denied that the city was a military objective and insisted that the border with Algeria was secure . Still, the episode reinforced perceptions in Algiers of a UAE-backed menace in its neighbourhood. Tensions continue to build. Algeria is increasingly concerned by Haftar’s influence in southern Libya, where his forces have tightened their grip on lucrative trafficking routes and strengthened cooperation with N’Djamena in fighting Chadian rebel groups. Haftar has thus obtained access to an important source of income and displaced Chadian rebels toward northern Niger, particularly the strategic Salvador Pass area , exacerbating instability near Algeria’s southern border. All in all, these developments help explain Algeria’s evolving approach to regional security. Rather than viewing events in Libya, Niger and Sudan separately, Algiers increasingly sees them as interconnected challenges. Containing the Clash What began as a downturn in Algerian-UAE relations has thus evolved into a full-blown crisis with possible reverberations across the northern third of Africa. Algeria has remained silent as to why precisely it severed diplomatic ties. The foreign ministry’s statement was vague , referring to “provocative or hostile” actions as well as warnings that had failed to deter Abu Dhabi from unspecified behaviour. Algeria may have avoided identifying grievances or conditions for reconciliation in order to allow for flexibility in future talks. The difficulty of substantiating its complaints may also have contributed to its ambiguous stance. To officials in Abu Dhabi, the break was both unanticipated and perplexing. Though he did not name Algeria, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, alluded to it in a tweet complaining of “ puzzles and signals that require decoding ” in interstate relations. The UAE foreign ministry adopted a more conciliatory tone, expressing hope that the rupture would prove temporary. A number of Emirati analysts said the dispute is of far greater significance to Algeria than to the UAE, given Abu Dhabi’s preoccupation with the war in the Gulf. These reactions underscore a divergence in perspectives: while Algiers views Abu Dhabi’s alliances as a growing threat to its regional influence, Abu Dhabi sees its engagement as part of a strategy driven by political, economic and security interests that go beyond any bilateral relationship. In reality, neither country can bar the other from an ever more cutthroat arena. Too, governments and armed groups in the region cannot be neatly categorised into two rival blocs; each of Niger, Chad and the assorted Libyan players has its own agenda that may not align precisely with either Algerian or Emirati wishes. Still, as Algeria assumes a more assertive stance and the UAE pursues its geographically expansive approach, seemingly oblivious to, or at least underestimating the depth of Algeria’s concerns and its conviction that Abu Dhabi is challenging its position, bilateral tensions risk becoming more fraught. Informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. The two countries would be far better served by taking steps and shifting their mindsets to help ensure that Emirati influence in Algeria’s neighbourhood, and Algiers’ response to it, do not become a trigger for bilateral confrontation. First, though full reconciliation may be out of reach for the moment, maintaining or restoring informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. Secondly, Algiers should avoid construing every Emirati undertaking in neighbouring countries as part of a strategy directed against its interests. Finally, Abu Dhabi ought to take Algeria’s security concerns more seriously. It should recognise that its regional partnerships, particularly those involving armed non-state actors, may threaten Algerian interests, even when not so intended. Both countries should have an interest in preventing local disputes from drawing them further toward confrontation, particularly given that both neighbouring governments and armed groups pursue agendas neither side can fully control. Absent such efforts, the rift could deepen, increasing the risk that local crises spiral into open hostility. The result would be to exacerbate tensions in a region already riven by deadly conflict. Lebanon: Amend Media Law to Protect Free Expression. Click to expand Image Lebanese lawmakers at the parliament building in downtown Beirut, January 9, 2025. © 2025 Hussein Malla/AP Photo (Beirut) – Lebanon’s parliament should amend the recently-adopted media law to fully remove all provisions in Lebanese law that restrict the right to free expression, Human Rights Watch said today. Parliament passed the law on August 11, 2026, but a new draft law introduced by 10 members of parliament on October 5 offers amendments to the law that would resolve its key problematic provisions. “Given the history of public officials and powerful individuals abusing Lebanon’s laws to clamp down on journalists, activists, and artists, parliament should act to prevent further abuse,” said Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch. “No one should face abusive retaliation for peacefully expressing their views, and parliament has a chance to end these abuses right here and now.” The media law, which parliament adopted after 16 years of deliberation, includes significant improvements. Some of the key advances include ending pretrial detention for free expression-related crimes committed online or through media-related means. The law establishes individuals’ right to create online media platforms or issue publications without prior state authorization and limits the military court’s jurisdiction over expression-related crimes committed online or through media-related means. It also decriminalizes defamation and insult in certain cases, transferring them to civil court jurisdiction. The law also includes provisions that would promote media independence, including by prohibiting undue interference in journalists’ work, promoting media workers’ rights to unionize, protecting sources’ anonymity, and limiting the ability of security services to search and seize journalists’ electronic equipment and documents. The adopted media law, however, includes a provision, article 104(b), which criminalizes the “intentional fabrication of falsehoods and dissemination of false and harmful news” providing for a sentence of up to three years in prison. For decades, Lebanese journalists, artists, media organizations, and civil society groups have repeatedly faced lawsuits based on criminal defamation charges and other vague legal provisions in retaliation for their work. This provision, which includes vague and undefined terms such as “harmful news,” risks enabling continued threats of criminal proceedings against journalists as well as such lawsuits. While the adopted media law decriminalizes defamation and insult in some cases, provisions found in Lebanon’s Penal Code, which the law does not mention, annul, or make inapplicable, would continue to criminalize libel, slander, and insult directed against a foreign state or its president, representatives, army, flag, or emblems. Such provisions also criminalize defamation against Lebanon’s president, state institutions, and army, among others, imposing prison sentences of up to two years. Provisions of the Lebanon Military Justice Code, which also remain in effect, include the criminalization of “publicly disparaging the flag or the army or infringing upon its dignity, reputation or morale,” imposing a prison sentence of up to three years. The amendments sought in the October 5 draft law would annul article 104(b) of the media law and make these articles, in both Lebanon’s Penal Code and Military Justice Code, inapplicable to cases covered by the media law, including for both media-related or online forms of expression.
